---
title: "Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models"
---

## Overview

A diffusion model splits the hard problem of sampling from a complex data distribution into two parts: an easy forward process that adds a little Gaussian noise many times, and a learned reverse process that undoes it. The forward process is fixed. It gradually erases the structure of the data until the state is close to a standard Gaussian. The reverse process starts from noise and is trained, as a neural network, to remove a little noise at every step [@ho2020].

This chapter develops that construction from first principles, following slides 2--25 of the lecture deck *Diffusion Model Theory* [@lecture-slides-diffusion]: the DDPM derivation on slides 2--16 and DDIM on slides 17--25. It begins with the probability tools needed to describe a latent Markov chain, derives the closed-form forward marginal and the variational training objective, and then turns the resulting Gaussian mean-matching problem into noise prediction. The relation among noise, data and velocity prediction makes the role of the loss weighting explicit. Finally, ancestral DDPM sampling is compared with the non-Markovian inference family and deterministic sampling rule of DDIM [@sohl2015; @ho2020; @ddim].

The construction rests on three mathematical facts.

1. Even after many Markov Gaussian transitions, $x_t$ at any time can be sampled from $x_0$ in a single step, in closed form.
2. Fitting the intractable reverse conditionals becomes, through a variational bound, a sum of Gaussian KL divergences that can be computed.
3. Predicting the noise $\epsilon$ that the forward process added, instead of the reverse mean, turns each term of the objective into a weighted mean squared error, which DDPM then simplifies to a plain one.

The exact reverse conditional is generally not Gaussian, but it becomes locally close to Gaussian when each forward step is small. This motivates the many-step DDPM construction. DDIM instead changes the inference path while preserving the same noisy marginals, which permits deterministic and shortened sampling trajectories [@ho2020; @ddim]. Short proofs follow the results they prove; longer verifications are collected in the appendix (@sec-proofs).

After reading this note you should be able to:

- derive the closed form of $q(x_t\mid x_0)$ from $q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})$;
- decompose the variational bound on the negative log-likelihood into $L_T$, $L_{t-1}$ and $L_0$;
- compute the mean and variance of $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$ by completing the square;
- show that mean prediction and noise prediction describe the same reverse mean, and derive the noise-estimation loss;
- reproduce the DDPM training and ancestral sampling algorithms, and explain why sampling adds noise back;
- explain what it means that the non-Markovian forward process of DDIM has the same marginals as DDPM.

## Notation

We follow the notation of the slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion], which for DDPM is that of @ho2020, except that vectors are written without boldface: $x_t$, $\epsilon$ and $\mu_\theta$. References of the form "slide 12" point to that deck, so that each section can be checked against the lecture. The symbols are collected in @tbl-notation.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $x_0\sim q_{\mathrm{data}}$ | clean sample from the data distribution, $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$ |
| $x_t$, $x_{a:b}$ | latent at noise level $t$ ($t=1,\ldots,T$); $x_{a:b}:=(x_a,\ldots,x_b)$ |
| $\beta_t\in(0,1)$ | variance of the noise added at step $t$ |
| $\alpha_t:=1-\beta_t$ | fraction of the signal kept in one step (in variance) |
| $\bar\alpha_t:=\prod_{s=1}^{t}\alpha_s$, $\bar\alpha_0:=1$ | signal fraction accumulated from time 0 to $t$ |
| $a_t:=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$, $b_t:=\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$ | signal and noise coefficients in $x_t=a_tx_0+b_t\epsilon$ |
| $\mathrm{SNR}(t):=\bar\alpha_t/(1-\bar\alpha_t)$ | signal-to-noise ratio at time $t$ |
| $\epsilon_t$, $z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ | noise of forward step $t$, and fresh noise of a sampling step; mutually independent |
| $\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$, $\bar\epsilon_t$ | noise of the one-step form $x_t=a_tx_0+b_t\epsilon$ (written $\bar\epsilon_t$ when its time matters); independent of $x_0$, but along one path a function of $\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_t$ |
| $q$, $q_t$, $q_\gamma$ | fixed forward diffusion, its marginal $q_t(x_t)$ at time $t$, and the DDIM family |
| $p_\theta$ | reverse generative model to be learned |
| $\tilde\mu_t,\tilde\beta_t$ | mean and variance of the exact forward posterior $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$ |
| $\mu_\theta,\epsilon_\theta,\hat x_0$ | reverse mean, noise prediction, and the data prediction computed from it |
| $\Sigma_\theta$, $s_\theta$ | covariance of the reverse transition, and the score estimate $-\epsilon_\theta/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$ |
| $\sigma_t^2$ | variance of the DDPM reverse transition |
| $w_t$ | coefficient of the noise-prediction MSE at time $t$ in the variational bound |
| $\gamma_t^2$ ($t\ge2$), $\gamma_1^2$ | posterior variance of the DDIM family $q_\gamma$; $\gamma_1^2>0$ is the variance of its decoder $p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)$ |
| $\eta$ | interpolation between DDIM ($\eta=0$) and DDPM ($\eta=1$) through $\gamma_t=\eta\sqrt{\tilde\beta_t}$ |
| $v$, $\phi_t$ | velocity target, and the angle with $a_t=\cos\phi_t$, $b_t=\sin\phi_t$ |
| $\mathcal N(x;m,\Sigma)$ | density at $x$ of a Gaussian with mean $m$ and covariance $\Sigma$ |

: Notation. {#tbl-notation}

Norms are Euclidean unless stated otherwise. $\mathbb E_q$ denotes expectation over $x_0\sim q_{\mathrm{data}}$ and all latents generated by the forward diffusion.

## Background: the Markov property and Gaussian tools

The derivation uses the KL divergence, Jensen's inequality and the evidence lower bound of a latent-variable model, which @sec-f-divergences and @sec-elbo-vae develop. It also uses the Markov property and a few Gaussian identities, which this section states before they are applied.

### Latent paths and the Markov factorization

The observed datum is a single $x_0$, but a diffusion model introduces latents $x_1,\ldots,x_T$ at increasing noise levels, so its likelihood $p_\theta(x_0)=\int p_\theta(x_{0:T})\,dx_{1:T}$ is bounded as for the variational autoencoder of Chapter 4, with two differences: the latent is a whole diffusion path rather than a single code, and the "encoder" $q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)$ is fixed rather than learned [@kingma2014; @ho2020].

::: {#def-markov}
## First-order Markov chain
A sequence $x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_T$ is a first-order Markov chain if for all $t=1,\ldots,T$

$$
q(x_t\mid x_{0:t-1})
=q(x_t\mid x_{t-1}).
$$ {#eq-markov-property}

Equivalently, $x_t\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}x_{0:t-2}\mid x_{t-1}$.
:::

Substituting @eq-markov-property into the chain rule gives $q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q(x_t\mid x_{0:t-1})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})$. This factorization defines the forward path distribution used below.

::: {#prp-reverse-markov}
## A Markov chain read backwards is still Markov
If the forward chain is Markov, then $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_{t:T})=q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ for all $t$. Proof in @sec-proof-reverse-markov.
:::

The **Markov property** of the reverse chain holds whatever the step size. What needs small steps is the approximation that the reverse transition $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ has a **Gaussian functional form**, which is discussed with the reverse process.

### Chapman--Kolmogorov composition and marginals

Integrating out intermediate states composes several transitions:

$$
q(x_t\mid x_0)
=\int q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)\,dx_{t-1}.
$$ {#eq-chapman-kolmogorov}

The first factor can be written $q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})$ instead of $q(x_t\mid x_{t-1},x_0)$ because of the Markov property. In DDPM both factors are linear Gaussian, so the integral is Gaussian too.

It is important to distinguish the **joint distribution of a path** from the **marginal at one time**. The product of Markov transitions fixes how the whole path is coupled, but knowing only $q(x_t\mid x_0)$ does not determine the coupling between different times. DDIM uses exactly this freedom: it keeps the same $q(x_t\mid x_0)$ as DDPM while using a non-Markovian path (@sec-ddim) [@ddim].

### Gaussian tools

Every closed form in this chapter follows from three lemmas. Their proofs are in @sec-proof-lemmas.

::: {#lem-gauss-lin}
## Linear combinations of independent Gaussians
If $u\sim\mathcal N(m_u,\Sigma_u)$ and $v\sim\mathcal N(m_v,\Sigma_v)$ are independent, then for constant matrices $A,B$ and a vector $c$,
$Au+Bv+c\sim\mathcal N\!\left(Am_u+Bm_v+c,\;A\Sigma_uA^{\mathsf T}+B\Sigma_vB^{\mathsf T}\right)$.
:::

::: {#lem-complete-square}
## Completing the square
If $A$ is symmetric positive definite and $h\in\mathbb R^d$, then

$$
-\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Ax+h^{\mathsf T}x
=-\tfrac12\left(x-A^{-1}h\right)^{\mathsf T}A\left(x-A^{-1}h\right)+\tfrac12h^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}h.
$$

Hence a density proportional to $\exp(-\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Ax+h^{\mathsf T}x)$ is $\mathcal N(A^{-1}h,\,A^{-1})$: **the quadratic coefficient is the precision, and the inverse precision times the linear coefficient is the mean**.
:::

::: {#lem-gauss-kl}
## KL divergence between isotropic Gaussians
If $q=\mathcal N(m_1,s_1^2I_d)$ and $p=\mathcal N(m_2,s_2^2I_d)$, then

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)
=\frac12\left[d\,\frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}+\frac{\lVert m_1-m_2\rVert^2}{s_2^2}-d+d\log\frac{s_2^2}{s_1^2}\right].
$$ {#eq-gauss-kl}

In particular, if $s_1=s_2=s$ then $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)=\lVert m_1-m_2\rVert^2/(2s^2)$.
:::

### Scope and assumptions

- $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$ is continuous and $q_{\mathrm{data}}$ has a finite second moment; only the discretized decoder of @sec-vlb-terms treats 8-bit data as discrete. Images are usually scaled to $[-1,1]$ per channel [@ho2020, Sec. 3.3].
- $T<\infty$, $0<\beta_t<1$, $\alpha_t=1-\beta_t$, and the noise schedule is fixed before training.
- The $\epsilon_t$ at different steps are $\mathcal N(0,I)$ samples independent of $x_0$ and of each other.
- Gaussian variances are positive. The degenerate endpoint $\tilde\beta_1=0$ at $t=1$ is handled by $L_0$.
- That the network represents the ideal conditional expectation is an idealization used for interpretation.

## Denoising diffusion probabilistic models {#sec-ddpm}

This section derives DDPM in six steps: the fixed forward process (@sec-forward), the reverse process and its variational bound (@sec-reverse), the tractable forward posterior (@sec-posterior), the change from mean prediction to noise prediction (@sec-noise-pred), the three equivalent prediction targets (@sec-parameterizations), and training and ancestral sampling (@sec-train-sample).

### The forward process {#sec-forward}

@fig-ddpm-process summarizes the structure of DDPM. The solid arrows $p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$, pointing right, form the learned generative chain from the standard Gaussian $x_T$ back to the data $x_0$; the dashed arrow $q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})$, pointing left, is the fixed forward transition from data to noise [@ho2020, Fig. 2].

![A fixed forward chain and a learned reverse chain on the same latents. Solid arrows are the learned transitions $p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ that turn noise into data; the dashed arrow is the fixed transition $q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})$ that adds noise. The thumbnails show a synthetic $64\times64$ image, drawn for this chapter from solid-colour shapes, as the data $x_0$, after $t-1=300$ and $t=301$ steps of the linear schedule, and as pure noise $x_T$.](figures/lec06/mumbumble-ddpm-graph.png){#fig-ddpm-process width=100%}

The forward direction repeatedly attenuates the previous state and adds noise until the state is close to a standard Gaussian. The reverse direction models each denoising step as a transition with parameters $\mu_\theta$ and $\Sigma_\theta$; applying these transitions from $x_T$ to $x_0$ produces a new sample rather than reconstructing a particular training example. Adding noise is fixed and tractable, whereas reversing the entropy increase requires information stored in the learned parameters. Small forward steps make a Gaussian approximation to each reverse transition plausible.

#### The forward chain

The forward process of DDPM (slide 4) is a Markov chain in the sense of @def-markov with Gaussian transitions [@ho2020, Eq. 2]

$$
q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)
=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q(x_t\mid x_{t-1}),
\qquad
q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})
=\mathcal N\!\left(\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1},\beta_t I\right)
=\mathcal N\!\left(\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1},\beta_t I\right).
$$ {#eq-forward-chain}

Reparameterizing the same transition gives

$$
x_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\epsilon_t,
\qquad \epsilon_t\sim\mathcal N(0,I).
$$ {#eq-forward-step}

The factor $\sqrt{\alpha_t}$ shrinks the previous signal and $\sqrt{\beta_t}$ adds fresh noise. Because $\alpha_t+\beta_t=1$, this step preserves unit covariance, as the energy computation below makes precise. The $\{\beta_t\}_{t=1}^{T}$ are not learned but fixed in advance. This finite variance schedule determines both the forward corruption levels and the coefficients used by the reverse model.

#### Jumping to any time in one step

$x_t$ can be sampled directly from $x_0$ without running the chain $t$ times. Unrolling @eq-forward-step twice, as on slide 5, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_t
&=\sqrt{\alpha_t}\left(
\sqrt{\alpha_{t-1}}x_{t-2}
+\sqrt{\beta_{t-1}}\epsilon_{t-1}
\right)
+\sqrt{\beta_t}\epsilon_t\\
&=\sqrt{\alpha_t\alpha_{t-1}}\,x_{t-2}
+\underbrace{\sqrt{\alpha_t\beta_{t-1}}\,\epsilon_{t-1}
+\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\epsilon_t}_{\sim\,\mathcal N(0,\,(1-\alpha_t\alpha_{t-1})I)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The sum of two independent Gaussian noises is again Gaussian, with variance $\alpha_t\beta_{t-1}+\beta_t=\alpha_t(1-\alpha_{t-1})+(1-\alpha_t)=1-\alpha_t\alpha_{t-1}$. Repeating this argument gives the following result.

::: {#prp-forward-marginal}
## Closed form of the forward marginal
For every $t=0,1,\ldots,T$ there is $\bar\epsilon_t\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$, independent of $x_0$, such that

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_t
&=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0
+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\bar\epsilon_t,
\qquad
\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s=1}^{t}\alpha_s,\\
\text{that is,}\quad
q(x_t\mid x_0)
&=\mathcal N\!\left(
\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0,
(1-\bar\alpha_t)I
\right).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-forward-marginal}
:::

*Proof.* By induction on $t$; at $t=0$, $\bar\alpha_0=1$ and the claim is trivial. Suppose that $x_{t-1}=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\bar\epsilon_{t-1}$, where $\bar\epsilon_{t-1}$ depends only on $\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_{t-1}$. Substituting into @eq-forward-step and using $\alpha_t\bar\alpha_{t-1}=\bar\alpha_t$,

$$
x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\Big(\sqrt{\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}\,\bar\epsilon_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\epsilon_t\Big).
$$

The two noises in the parentheses are independent of each other and of $x_0$, so by @lem-gauss-lin the parenthesis is Gaussian with mean 0 and covariance $\big[\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})+\beta_t\big]I=(1-\bar\alpha_t)I$, as in the two-step computation above. Writing it as $\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\bar\epsilon_t$ gives $\bar\epsilon_t\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$, independent of $x_0$. Equivalently, substituting the induction hypothesis into @eq-chapman-kolmogorov evaluates a Gaussian integral with the same result. $\square$

This sample representation is the **one-step renoising formula**:

$$
x_t
=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0
+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon,
\qquad \epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I).
$$ {#eq-one-step-renoising}

It matters a great deal for training: after drawing any $t$, $x_t$ is built with one Gaussian draw, without generating the intermediate states $x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1}$. As $t$ grows and $\bar\alpha_t\to0$, the data component disappears and $q(x_T\mid x_0)\approx\mathcal N(0,I)$, so generation can start from $x_T\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$. Multiplying the Markov transitions has therefore produced a direct transition from $x_0$ to any selected time $t$.

#### Energy, the noise schedule and the SNR {#sec-schedule}

**What "keeping the energy" means.** Let $\Sigma_{t-1}$ be the covariance of $x_{t-1}$. Since $\epsilon_t$ is independent of $x_{t-1}$, the covariance of the sum in @eq-forward-step is the sum of the two covariances; no Gaussian assumption on $x_{t-1}$ is needed. Hence

$$
\Sigma_t=\alpha_t\Sigma_{t-1}+\beta_tI
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Sigma_t-I=\alpha_t(\Sigma_{t-1}-I)
=\bar\alpha_t(\Sigma_0-I).
$$

If the data have unit covariance, the covariance stays $I$ at every step (variance preserving); otherwise $\Sigma_t\to I$ as $\bar\alpha_t\to0$. The mean is $\mathbb E x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\mathbb E x_0\to0$.

**The linear schedule and the signal-to-noise ratio.** The size of one step is set by $\beta_t$, but the signal left at time $t$ is set by $\bar\alpha_t$, and the corresponding signal-to-noise ratio is $\mathrm{SNR}(t)=\bar\alpha_t/(1-\bar\alpha_t)$. The original paper uses a linear schedule from $\beta_1=10^{-4}$ to $\beta_T=0.02$ with $T=1000$ [@ho2020, Sec. 4]. As @fig-noise-schedule shows, $\beta_t$ is linear but $\bar\alpha_t$ decays nonlinearly: signal and noise variances become equal ($\bar\alpha_t=\tfrac12$) between $t=259$ and $t=260$, and $\bar\alpha_T\approx4.0\times10^{-5}$. The SNR spans more than eight orders of magnitude, from about $10^4$ at $t=1$ to $4\times10^{-5}$ at $t=T$, and a uniform $t$ covers them unevenly: the four decades above $\mathrm{SNR}=1$ get only the first 259 steps, the remaining 4.4 decades the other 741.

![A linear $\beta_t$ removes the signal nonlinearly. (a) The per-step variance $\beta_t$ of the original DDPM ($T=1000$) is linear. (b) The coefficients $a_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$ and $b_t=\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$ of the one-step renoising formula cross between $t=259$ and $t=260$ (dotted line at $t=259$), so half of the signal variance is gone after about a quarter of the chain. (c) $\mathrm{SNR}(t)$ falls through more than eight orders of magnitude, from about $10^{4}$ to $4\times10^{-5}$. Schedule of @ho2020, Sec. 4; curves from `curves()` in @sec-schedule-code.](figures/lec06/mumbumble-noise-schedule.png){#fig-noise-schedule width=100%}

**Other schedules.** @nichol2021 [Sec. 3.2] prescribe $\bar\alpha_t$ directly by the cosine schedule $\bar\alpha_t=f(t)/f(0)$, $f(t)=\cos^2\!\big(\tfrac{t/T+s}{1+s}\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{2}\big)$ with $s=0.008$, and set $\beta_t=1-\bar\alpha_t/\bar\alpha_{t-1}$, clipped at 0.999. It destroys information more gradually: with $T=1000$ its $\bar\alpha_t$ is closest to $\tfrac12$ at $t=496$, against $t=259$ for the linear schedule (@sec-schedule-code). A schedule is thus best seen as a design of the path of $\bar\alpha_t$, that is, of the SNR, rather than of $\beta_t$ itself.

### The reverse process and the variational bound {#sec-reverse}

#### The generative model

The reverse generative model is

$$
p_\theta(x_{0:T})
=p(x_T)\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t),
$$ {#eq-reverse-joint}

with $p(x_T)=\mathcal N(0,I)$ and, as in @ho2020, Eq. 1, and on slide 6, each reverse transition modelled as

$$
p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
=\mathcal N\!\left(
\mu_\theta(x_t,t),
\Sigma_\theta(x_t,t)
\right).
$$

A common choice fixes $\Sigma_\theta(x_t,t)=\sigma_t^2I$ from the forward schedule and predicts only the mean. The time index is an explicit input because the noise level changes throughout the chain; @ho2020 [Sec. 4] feed $t$ to a U-Net through a sinusoidal position embedding. The exact reverse conditional need not be Gaussian. Slide 6 states that in the limit of small steps it has the same functional form as the forward process; the next subsection explains why, and why large jumps require more care.

#### Why the reverse transition is nearly Gaussian for small steps {#sec-small-step}

In Bayes' rule $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\propto q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\,q_{t-1}(x_{t-1})$, the first factor is a narrow Gaussian of width $\sqrt{\beta_t/\alpha_t}$. Expanding $\log q_{t-1}$ to first order inside that region and applying @lem-complete-square gives the heuristic approximation (derived in @sec-proof-small-step)

$$
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
\approx
\mathcal N\!\left(
\frac{x_t}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}+\frac{\beta_t}{\alpha_t}\nabla\log q_{t-1}\!\Big(\frac{x_t}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big),\;
\frac{\beta_t}{\alpha_t}I
\right).
$$ {#eq-reverse-small-step}

One reverse step undoes the forward shrinkage, moves along the score $\nabla\log q_{t-1}$ (the gradient of the log-density) of the marginal, and carries noise of the same size as the forward step. The approximation keeps the slope of $\log q_{t-1}$ across one step and drops its curvature. For sharply concentrated data the dropped term has relative size of the order of

$$
\frac{\beta_t}{\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}
=\frac{\mathrm{SNR}(t-1)}{\mathrm{SNR}(t)}-1,
$$ {#eq-small-step-ratio}

the relative drop of the SNR over one step. The error has two sources.

- *Gaussian data.* The exact reverse conditional is Gaussian, but the variance of @eq-reverse-small-step is too large by a relative amount that is at most this ratio, and reaches it as the data variance goes to zero; the mean errs only at second order (@sec-proof-small-step).
- *Non-Gaussian data.* The exact reverse conditional is not Gaussian at all. If $\log q_{t-1}$ is smooth, with curvature bounded on the scale $\sqrt{\beta_t}$ of one step, this error comes from the dropped higher-order terms of the expansion and also vanishes as $\beta_t\to0$.

Both errors are small when **the noise variance of one step is much smaller than the noise variance accumulated so far**. This is a scale rather than a sharp condition, since between well-separated modes the curvature of $\log q_{t-1}$ can be larger. For the linear schedule the ratio is largest at $t=2$, about 1.2, and at $t=1$ it is undefined, so the last step $x_1\to x_0$ is the hardest to approximate by a Gaussian.

#### An upper bound on the negative log-likelihood

The goal is a small negative log-likelihood. Multiplying and dividing by the forward path distribution, as on slide 7, gives

$$
p_\theta(x_0)
=\int p_\theta(x_{0:T})\,dx_{1:T}
=\int q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)
\frac{p_\theta(x_{0:T})}{q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)}\,dx_{1:T}
=\mathbb E_{q}\!\left[
\frac{p_\theta(x_{0:T})}{q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)}
\right],
$$

and by Jensen's inequality

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[-\log p_\theta(x_0)\right]
\le
\mathbb E_q\!\left[
-\log\frac{p_\theta(x_{0:T})}{q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)}
\right]
=:\mathcal L_{\mathrm{VLB}}.
$$ {#eq-vlb}

Minimizing $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{VLB}}$ therefore minimizes an upper bound on the negative log-likelihood. Substituting $p_\theta(x_{0:T})=p_\theta(x_0)\,p_\theta(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)$ shows that for fixed $x_0$ the gap of the bound is $D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)\,\Vert\,p_\theta(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)\big)$, so the bound is tight only when the forward path distribution equals the model's posterior over paths.

#### Decomposing the variational bound

::: {#thm-vlb}
## Decomposition of the variational bound
For @eq-forward-chain and @eq-reverse-joint,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{VLB}}
&=\underbrace{
\mathbb E_q\!\left[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q(x_T\mid x_0)\,\Vert\,p(x_T)\right)
\right]}_{L_T}\\
&\quad+
\sum_{t=2}^{T}
\underbrace{
\mathbb E_q\!\left[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)
\,\Vert\,
p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
\right)
\right]}_{L_{t-1}}\\
&\quad+
\underbrace{
\mathbb E_q\!\left[-\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)\right]
}_{L_0}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-vlb-decomposition}
:::

The algebra of slides 7--9 turns @eq-vlb into @eq-vlb-decomposition in three steps; the full proof with every change of measure justified is in @sec-proof-vlb.

First, substituting @eq-forward-chain and @eq-reverse-joint, the loss is

$$
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{VLB}}
=\mathbb E_q\!\left[
-\log p(x_T)
-\sum_{t\ge1}
\log\frac{p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)}{q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})}
\right].
$$ {#eq-vlb-sum}

Next, the Markov property and Bayes' rule rewrite the denominator for $t\ge2$:

$$
q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})
=q(x_t\mid x_{t-1},x_0)
=q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)
\frac{q(x_t\mid x_0)}{q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)}.
$$ {#eq-bayes-rearrange}

Setting the $t=1$ term aside and substituting this identity for $t\ge2$, the terms $\log q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)-\log q(x_t\mid x_0)$ telescope (slide 8):

$$
\sum_{t\ge1}\log\frac{p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)}{q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})}
=\sum_{t=2}^{T}\log\frac{p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)}{q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)}
+\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)
-\log q(x_T\mid x_0).
$$

The telescoping sum is why all intermediate marginal-density terms disappear. Substituting it into @eq-vlb-sum and reading the expectations under $q$ of the log-ratios as KL divergences gives @eq-vlb-decomposition.

The roles of the terms are as follows. $L_T$ measures how close the last forward distribution is to the prior and does not depend on $\theta$. $L_{t-1}$ matches one reverse step to the computable exact posterior; it is the main training signal of DDPM. The target $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$ can be computed during training because $x_0$ is known. $L_0$ is the negative log-likelihood of the final reconstruction $x_1\to x_0$. The Markov factorization and telescoping identity are what reduce a path-space expectation to this sum of local terms.

@fig-elbo-decomposition shows where on the chain each kind of term sits.

![Where each term of the bound sits on the chain. $L_T$ compares the end of the forward chain with the prior and contains no parameters; each $L_{t-1}$ is a Gaussian-to-Gaussian KL divergence at one interior transition; $L_0$ scores the final reconstruction in data space. Solid arrows are the learned transitions $p_\theta$, grey dashed arrows the fixed transitions $q$, and the blue dotted arrow marks that the target $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$ also conditions on the clean $x_0$.](figures/lec06/mumbumble-elbo-decomposition.png){#fig-elbo-decomposition width=100%}

#### The end terms of the bound {#sec-vlb-terms}

**The prior term $L_T$.** $L_T$ has a closed form. Substituting $m_1=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_T}x_0$, $s_1^2=1-\bar\alpha_T$, $m_2=0$, $s_2^2=1$ into @lem-gauss-kl,

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q(x_T\mid x_0)\,\Vert\,\mathcal N(0,I)\right)
=\frac12\left[\bar\alpha_T\left(\lVert x_0\rVert^2-d\right)-d\log(1-\bar\alpha_T)\right]
\approx\frac12\bar\alpha_T\lVert x_0\rVert^2.
$$

Since $\lVert x_0\rVert^2\le d$ for data scaled to $[-1,1]^d$, the bracket is at most $-d\log(1-\bar\alpha_T)$, so $L_T\le-\tfrac d2\log(1-\bar\alpha_T)$. Per dimension, $L_T/d\le-\tfrac12\log(1-\bar\alpha_T)\approx2.0\times10^{-5}$ nats $\approx2.9\times10^{-5}$ bits, and @ho2020 report about $10^{-5}$ bits/dim on real data (Sec. 4). The cost of $q(x_T\mid x_0)\approx\mathcal N(0,I)$ is negligible.

**The decoder term $L_0$.** @ho2020 scale the 8-bit pixel values $\{0,\ldots,255\}$ linearly to $[-1,1]$, so neighbouring values are $2/255$ apart, and use the discrete decoder (Sec. 3.3, Eq. 13)

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)
&=\prod_{i=1}^{d}\int_{\delta_-(x_0^i)}^{\delta_+(x_0^i)}
\mathcal N\!\left(x;\mu_\theta^i(x_1,1),\sigma_1^2\right)dx,\\
\delta_+(x)
&=
\begin{cases}
\infty, & x=1,\\
x+\tfrac{1}{255}, & x<1,
\end{cases}\\
\delta_-(x)
&=
\begin{cases}
-\infty, & x=-1,\\
x-\tfrac{1}{255}, & x>-1.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-discrete-decoder}

where $i$ indexes the coordinates. Each factor is the probability of the bin of width $2/255$ around the observed value, with the two edge bins extended to infinity, so $L_0$, and with it the whole bound, is a code length for discrete data; @eq-vlb then bounds a discrete negative log-likelihood by the same Jensen argument. The decoder needs its own positive variance $\sigma_1^2$, because the choice $\sigma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$ adopted below gives $\tilde\beta_1=0$; for concreteness this chapter takes $\sigma_1^2=\beta_1$. This is a convention of the chapter, not a value stated by @ho2020; any value of the same order, such as $\tilde\beta_2\approx5.5\times10^{-5}$, behaves the same way below.

### The forward posterior {#sec-posterior}

Computing $L_{t-1}$ requires $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$. As on slide 10, Bayes' rule and the Markov property give

$$
\begin{aligned}
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)
&=\frac{
q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\,q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)
}{q(x_t\mid x_0)}\\
&=\frac{\mathcal N(x_t;\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1},\beta_tI)\;\mathcal N(x_{t-1};\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0,(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})I)}{\mathcal N(x_t;\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0,(1-\bar\alpha_t)I)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The numerator is a product of two Gaussians, the second of which is the one-step marginal @eq-forward-marginal, and the denominator does not depend on $x_{t-1}$. Expanding the squared norms in the exponents and keeping only the terms that contain $x_{t-1}$,

$$
\log q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)
=-\frac12\left(\frac{\alpha_t}{\beta_t}+\frac{1}{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\right)\lVert x_{t-1}\rVert^2
+\left(\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}{\beta_t}x_t+\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}}{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0\right)^{\!\mathsf T}x_{t-1}
+\text{const},
$$

and completing the square (@lem-complete-square) gives the following (slides 10--11).

::: {#prp-posterior}
## Forward posterior
For $t\ge2$, $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)=\mathcal N\!\left(\tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0),\tilde\beta_tI\right)$ with

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0)
&=\frac{
\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,x_t
+\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,\\
\tilde\beta_t
&=\frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\beta_t.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-posterior-mean}
:::

*Proof.* By @lem-complete-square the precision is the coefficient of $-\tfrac12\lVert x_{t-1}\rVert^2$ above and the variance is its inverse. Putting the precision over a common denominator and using $\bar\alpha_t=\alpha_t\bar\alpha_{t-1}$ and $\alpha_t+\beta_t=1$,

$$
\frac{\alpha_t}{\beta_t}+\frac{1}{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}
=\frac{\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})+\beta_t}{\beta_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}
=\frac{1-\bar\alpha_t}{\beta_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}=\frac{1}{\tilde\beta_t}.
$$

The mean is the variance $\tilde\beta_t$ times the linear coefficient, and multiplying out, $\tilde\beta_t\sqrt{\alpha_t}/\beta_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})/(1-\bar\alpha_t)$ and $\tilde\beta_t\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}/(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\beta_t/(1-\bar\alpha_t)$. $\square$

It is important that this distribution is conditioned on the clean $x_0$ as well as on $x_t$. During training $x_0$ is known, so the target can be computed; during generation it is not, so $p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ has to approximate the resulting reverse conditional. DDIM will preserve the same noisy marginals while changing how the latent path depends on $x_0$.

#### Choice of the reverse variance

Slide 13 fixes the reverse variance to $\sigma_t^2:=\tilde\beta_t$, one of the two fixed choices of @ho2020 [Sec. 3.2]; the other is $\sigma_t^2=\beta_t$. The former is optimal when $x_0$ is a single point, the latter when $x_0\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$, and the two give similar results. Neither is chosen freely at each step: the forward schedule $\{\beta_t\}$ determines both in closed form. Their ratio $\tilde\beta_t/\beta_t=(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})/(1-\bar\alpha_t)$ is close to 1 except at small $t$ [@nichol2021, Sec. 3.1, Fig. 1], the same region where the Gaussian approximation of @sec-small-step is worst. At $t=1$, $\tilde\beta_1=0$ means that the forward posterior is a point mass, not that a logarithm of 0 must be computed; this endpoint is handled by $L_0$, and the sampler sets $z=0$ at the last step.

### From mean prediction to noise prediction {#sec-noise-pred}

#### Simplifying the Gaussian KL divergence

With the reverse variance fixed, $L_{t-1}$ is a KL divergence between two Gaussians: one is the posterior computed from the real data, the other the parameterized model to be estimated by a neural network. Choosing different variances leaves an additional variance term; choosing them equal leaves only **the squared distance between the means** (@lem-gauss-kl). Hence (slide 12)

$$
L_{t-1}
=\mathbb E_q\!\left[
\frac{1}{2\sigma_t^2}
\left\lVert
\tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0)-\mu_\theta(x_t,t)
\right\rVert^2
\right]
+C_t,
$$ {#eq-mean-matching}

where $C_t\ge0$ is a constant independent of $\theta$ that vanishes when $\sigma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$ (@sec-proof-kl-constant).

#### Replacing the dependence on the data by the noise

The target $\tilde\mu_t$ in @eq-mean-matching depends on $x_0$, which the network has to infer from $x_t$ at generation time. As on slide 12, inverting the one-step renoising formula @eq-one-step-renoising rewrites that dependence as one on the noise, so that the network can be asked to predict the noise instead:
$x_0=(x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$. Substituting this expression into @eq-posterior-mean,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tilde\mu_t
&=\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})\,x_t+\beta_t\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}}\left(x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon\right)}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\\
&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(\frac{\alpha_t-\bar\alpha_t+\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,x_t-\frac{\beta_t\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon\right)
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}
\left(
x_t-
\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\epsilon
\right).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-posterior-mean-epsilon}

The second line factors out $1/\sqrt{\alpha_t}$ using $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}=1/\sqrt{\alpha_t}$ and $\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})=(\alpha_t-\bar\alpha_t)/\sqrt{\alpha_t}$; the last equality holds because $\alpha_t+\beta_t=1$ makes the numerator $1-\bar\alpha_t$. The exact posterior mean is now expressed through $x_t$ and the noise $\epsilon$ that produced it.

#### The noise parameterization and its loss

$\tilde\mu_t$ is a training target computed from the data, whereas the network estimates $\mu_\theta$. Following @eq-posterior-mean-epsilon, the network can be parameterized to predict the noise $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ instead of the mean (slide 13):

$$
\mu_\theta(x_t,t)
:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}
\left(
x_t-
\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}
\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)
\right).
$$ {#eq-epsilon-parameterization}

The difference of the two means is a constant multiple of the difference of the noises,

$$
\tilde\mu_t-\mu_\theta
=\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\left(\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)-\epsilon\right).
$$

Substituting this relation into @eq-mean-matching and replacing the expectation over $x_t$ by one over $(x_0,\epsilon)$ through @eq-one-step-renoising gives the loss of slide 13,

$$
\begin{aligned}
L_{t-1}
&=w_t\,
\mathbb E_{x_0,\epsilon}\!\left[
\left\lVert
\epsilon-
\epsilon_\theta\!\left(
\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0
+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon,
t
\right)
\right\rVert^2
\right]
+C_t,\\
w_t
&:=\frac{\beta_t^2}
{2\sigma_t^2\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_t)}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-eps-loss}

This trains the network to estimate the noise used to construct $x_t$ at the selected noise level. The noise-prediction MSE is therefore not an arbitrary surrogate: it is the Gaussian reverse-mean matching objective written in observable training variables.

#### The simplified objective

In practice DDPM drops the time coefficient $w_t$ of @eq-eps-loss and trains on the following objective, the loss minimized by Algorithm 1 on slide 14 [@ho2020, Eq. 14]:

$$
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}
=\mathbb E_{\substack{
x_0\sim q_{\mathrm{data}},\\
t\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{1,\ldots,T\},\\
\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)
}}
\left[
\left\lVert
\epsilon-
\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)
\right\rVert^2
\right],
\quad
x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0
+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon.
$$ {#eq-simple-loss}

#### The simplified objective is a reweighted ELBO {#sec-reweighting}

Dropping $w_t$ changes how training effort is distributed over noise levels. The next calculation makes explicit what changes, what stays fixed at the population optimum, and why the reweighting can improve samples.

**What changes.** Apart from the end terms $L_T$ and $L_0$, discussed below, $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{VLB}}$ is $\sum_{t\ge2}w_t\,\mathbb E\lVert\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta\rVert^2$ plus a constant, and $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}$ replaces every $w_t$ by 1, up to the factor $1/T$ from averaging over $t$ (its $t=1$ term corresponds to $L_0$, as shown below). For the two fixed variance choices,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sigma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t:&\quad
w_t=\frac{\beta_t^2(1-\bar\alpha_t)}{2\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_t)(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})\beta_t}
=\frac{\beta_t}{2\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})},\\
\sigma_t^2=\beta_t:&\quad
w_t=\frac{\beta_t}{2\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_t)}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-wt-simplified}

The ratio $\beta_t/(\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}))$ in the first expression is the ratio @eq-small-step-ratio that set the heuristic error scale of the Gaussian approximation in @sec-small-step. Written with the SNR,

$$
w_t=\frac12\left(\frac{\mathrm{SNR}(t-1)}{\mathrm{SNR}(t)}-1\right)
\qquad(\sigma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t),
$$ {#eq-wt-snr}

so the exact VLB weights the noise-prediction error at each step by the relative loss of SNR in that step. @tbl-vlb-weights quantifies this for the linear schedule. With $\sigma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$ the weight at $t=2$ is about 59 times the mean, and for $t\le100$ it decays roughly like $1/t$ (@fig-vlb-weights). The first 1% of the chain carries 18.4% of the total weight, against 0.9% under $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}$. The exact VLB thus concentrates the training signal on easy denoising problems with almost no noise, and $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}$ sharply lowers their share.

| $\sigma_t^2$ / loss | $t=2$ | $t=10$ | $t=100$ | $t=500$ | share of $t\le10$ | share of $t\le100$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| VLB, $\tilde\beta_t$ | 58.9 | 8.49 | 1.01 | 0.54 | 18.4% | 39.2% |
| VLB, $\beta_t$ | 29.1 | 7.87 | 1.08 | 0.59 | 12.8% | 34.1% |
| $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}$ | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0.9% | 9.9% |

: Weights of the interior terms $t=2,\ldots,T$ for the linear schedule ($T=1000$); the $t=1$ term is $L_0$, whose coefficient $w_1$ is undefined for $\sigma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$ because $\tilde\beta_1=0$. The first four columns give $w_t$ divided by its mean; the last two give the share of the total weight carried by $t\le10$ and by $t\le100$. Computed by the code in @sec-schedule-code. {#tbl-vlb-weights}

![The exact bound puts most of its weight on the first few steps. The time coefficients $w_t$ of @eq-wt-simplified for both fixed variance choices, normalized to mean 1 over $t=2,\ldots,T$ (linear schedule, $T=1000$, log scales), reach tens of times the average at small $t$ and decay roughly like $1/t$; $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}$ (dotted) weights all times equally. Values in @tbl-vlb-weights.](figures/lec06/mumbumble-vlb-weights.png){#fig-vlb-weights width=95%}

**What does not change.** If the network can represent an arbitrary function of $x_t$ for each $t$, then for any positive weights $\{\lambda_t\}$ the minimizer of $\sum_t\lambda_t\mathbb E\lVert\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\rVert^2$ is the same,

$$
\epsilon^*(x_t,t)=\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t]
$$ {#eq-bayes-optimal}

(@sec-proof-bayes). The weights matter only in the practical situation where **one finite network is shared across all $t$**: they decide how capacity and gradient are allocated across noise levels.

**What it buys.** @ho2020 explain that the simplified loss lowers the weight of the small-$t$ terms, the easy tasks of removing very little noise, so that the network can focus on the harder denoising tasks at larger $t$, and that this improves sample quality (Sec. 3.4). On CIFAR-10, training on the exact VLB with a fixed isotropic variance gave IS 7.67, FID 13.51 and NLL $\le$ 3.70 bits/dim, while $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}$ gave IS 9.46, FID 3.17 and NLL $\le$ 3.75 bits/dim [@ho2020, Tables 1--2]. The reweighting **trades a little log-likelihood for a large gain in sample quality**. This benefit is empirical: the numerical examples of this chapter use the Bayes-optimal predictor, for which the weights do not matter (@eq-bayes-optimal), so they cannot show it; @nichol2021 recover much of the lost likelihood by also learning the variance.

The ablation of @ho2020 [Sec. 4.2, Table 2] shows why the noise parameterization matters: predicting $\tilde\mu_t$ works only with the true bound (FID 13.22 with a fixed isotropic variance; its unweighted MSE was unstable), whereas predicting $\epsilon$ is about as good under the bound (FID 13.51) and much better under $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}$ (FID 3.17).

**Learning the variance.** The constant $C_t$ of @eq-mean-matching is independent of $\theta$ only because the variance is fixed. @nichol2021 instead learn a diagonal $\Sigma_\theta(x_t,t)$ with entries $\exp\!\big(\nu\log\beta_t+(1-\nu)\log\tilde\beta_t\big)$, an interpolation in the log domain between the two fixed choices, where the network outputs one $\nu$ per dimension (Sec. 3.1). The variance term $C_t$ of the KL divergence then depends on $\theta$ and trains $\nu$. They minimize $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{hybrid}}=\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}+0.001\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{VLB}}$ with a stop-gradient on the mean inside $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{VLB}}$, so the mean keeps the reweighting of $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}$ while the bound trains the variance. The rest of this chapter keeps the variance fixed, as on the slides.

**Why not optimize the bound directly?** Besides sample quality there is an optimization reason. The terms of the bound differ by orders of magnitude (@tbl-vlb-weights), so with $t$ drawn uniformly its gradient is very noisy. @nichol2021 keep the bound but sample $t$ with probability proportional to $\sqrt{\mathbb E[L_{t-1}^2]}$ and divide each term by that probability, which leaves the bound unbiased and makes it far less noisy to optimize (Sec. 3.3).

**The end terms.** The weights $w_t$ above apply only to the interior KL terms, $t\ge2$; $L_T$ does not depend on $\theta$. If each bin integral of @eq-discrete-decoder is approximated by density times bin width, $-\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)$ becomes $\lVert x_0-\mu_\theta(x_1,1)\rVert^2/(2\sigma_1^2)$ plus a constant. At $t=1$, $x_1=\sqrt{\alpha_1}x_0+\sqrt{\beta_1}\epsilon$ and @eq-epsilon-parameterization give $x_0-\mu_\theta(x_1,1)=\sqrt{\beta_1/\alpha_1}\,(\epsilon_\theta-\epsilon)$, so

$$
L_0\approx\frac{\beta_1}{2\alpha_1\sigma_1^2}\,
\mathbb E\lVert\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_1,1)\rVert^2+\text{const},
$$

formally a noise-prediction MSE with weight $1/(2\alpha_1)\approx\tfrac12$ for $\sigma_1^2=\beta_1$: up to this weight, the $t=1$ term of $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}$ [@ho2020, Sec. 3.4]. The approximation gives the form of the term rather than its value, since the bin width $2/255\approx0.0078$ is not small next to $\sigma_1=0.01$.

**Where the bound spends its nats.** @fig-variance-vlb shows the small-$t$ concentration from two sides: in (a), the two fixed variances $\tilde\beta_t$ and $\beta_t$ differ only in the first steps; in (b), the interior terms $L_{t-1}$, computed exactly for the one-dimensional example of @sec-experiments, fall by six orders of magnitude, as the weights of @tbl-vlb-weights predict. @nichol2021 report the same pattern for a trained image model (Fig. 2).
