(a) The ratio $\tilde\beta_t/\beta_t$ for the linear schedule shortened to $T=100,250,500,1000$ steps (both endpoints of $\beta_t$ multiplied by $1000/T$) is close to 1 except for the first steps. (b) The interior VLB terms $L_{t-1}$ of the one-dimensional mixture of @sec-experiments with the Bayes-optimal predictor and $\sigma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$ (log axes) fall by six orders of magnitude, and $t\le10$ carries 42.6% of their total. Panel (a) from `curves()` in @sec-schedule-code, panel (b) from `vlb_terms()` in the code of @sec-experiments.](figures/lec06/mumbumble-variance-vlb.png){#fig-variance-vlb width=100%}

### Noise, data and velocity prediction {#sec-parameterizations}

Diffusion models can predict the noise $\epsilon$, the clean data $x_0$, or the velocity $v$. These targets are algebraically interchangeable, but the corresponding MSE objectives weight reconstruction errors differently across noise levels [@salimans2022, Sec. 4 and App. D].

With $a_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$ and $b_t=\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$ we have $x_t=a_tx_0+b_t\epsilon$ and $a_t^2+b_t^2=1$.

#### Noise prediction and data prediction

If the network outputs $\hat\epsilon=\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$, the data prediction is

$$
\hat x_0
=\frac{x_t-b_t\hat\epsilon}{a_t},
$$ {#eq-epsilon-to-x0}

and if it outputs $\hat x_0$ directly instead,

$$
\hat\epsilon
=\frac{x_t-a_t\hat x_0}{b_t}.
$$ {#eq-x0-to-epsilon}

The two are algebraically equivalent at interior times with $a_t,b_t>0$. But at very low SNR, $a_t\approx0$ and the $1/a_t$ in @eq-epsilon-to-x0 strongly amplifies errors in the noise prediction; at very high SNR, $b_t\approx0$ and the $1/b_t$ in @eq-x0-to-epsilon strongly amplifies errors in the data prediction. Even though they represent the same ideal solution, the conditioning of training differs at finite precision and capacity. For the same reason samplers often clip the data prediction to the data range, $\hat x_0\leftarrow\mathrm{clip}(\hat x_0,-1,1)$, before it is used; this static thresholding keeps samples in range but departs from the exact noise-parameterized mean [@saharia2022, Sec. 2.3, arXiv:2205.11487].

Whichever target is predicted, the DDPM reverse mean is the posterior mean of @eq-posterior-mean evaluated at the data prediction, $\mu_\theta(x_t,t)=\tilde\mu_t(x_t,\hat x_0)$: substituting @eq-epsilon-to-x0 for $x_0$ is exactly the computation of @eq-posterior-mean-epsilon and gives back @eq-epsilon-parameterization. For the same underlying prediction the three parameterizations therefore define the same sampler; they differ only in what the network is asked to output.

#### Velocity prediction is an orthogonal rotation

Since $a_t^2+b_t^2=1$, define the angle $\phi_t:=\arctan(b_t/a_t)\in(0,\pi/2)$, so that $a_t=\cos\phi_t$ and $b_t=\sin\phi_t$. The velocity target is defined as

$$
v:=a_t\epsilon-b_tx_0
=\frac{d x_t}{d\phi_t}\bigg|_{x_0,\epsilon\ \text{fixed}}.
$$

The second equality follows by differentiating $x_t=\cos\phi_t\,x_0+\sin\phi_t\,\epsilon$ with respect to $\phi_t$, which explains the name "velocity" [@salimans2022, App. D]. In matrix form,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x_t\\v\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
a_t & b_t\\
-b_t & a_t
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}x_0\\\epsilon\end{bmatrix},
$$

the two rows are orthogonal and the determinant is $a_t^2+b_t^2=1$, so the matrix is a rotation: $(x_t,v)$ are the coordinates of the pair $(x_0,\epsilon)$ along axes turned by the angle $\phi_t$. The inverse is the transpose,

$$
x_0=a_tx_t-b_tv,
\qquad
\epsilon=b_tx_t+a_tv.
$$ {#eq-v-inverse}

For small $t$, $a_t\approx1$ and $v\approx\epsilon$; for large $t$, $b_t\approx1$ and $v\approx-x_0$. A $v$-predicting network enters the sampler through $\hat x_0=a_tx_t-b_t\hat v$, that is, through $\tilde\mu_t(x_t,\hat x_0)$ as above.

This is why @salimans2022 introduced $v$-prediction for progressive distillation (Sec. 4). A distilled sampler takes a few large steps and evaluates the network close to $\mathrm{SNR}=0$, where @eq-epsilon-to-x0 amplifies the error of $\hat\epsilon$ by $b_t/a_t\to\infty$, whereas $\hat x_0=a_tx_t-b_t\hat v$ from @eq-v-inverse stays bounded.

#### Same error, different weights

Converting one prediction into another at the same $(x_t,t)$, @eq-epsilon-to-x0 and @eq-v-inverse give $\epsilon-\hat\epsilon=\tfrac{a_t}{b_t}(\hat x_0-x_0)$ and $x_0-\hat x_0=-b_t(v-\hat v)$, hence

$$
\left\lVert\epsilon-\hat\epsilon\right\rVert^2
=\frac{a_t^2}{b_t^2}
\left\lVert x_0-\hat x_0\right\rVert^2
=a_t^2\left\lVert v-\hat v\right\rVert^2.
$$ {#eq-parameterization-error-scaling}

Since $a_t^2/b_t^2=\mathrm{SNR}(t)$ and $1/b_t^2=1+\mathrm{SNR}(t)$,

$$
\lVert\epsilon-\hat\epsilon\rVert^2=\mathrm{SNR}(t)\,\lVert x_0-\hat x_0\rVert^2,
\qquad
\lVert v-\hat v\rVert^2=\big(1+\mathrm{SNR}(t)\big)\lVert x_0-\hat x_0\rVert^2.
$$

Concretely, Algorithm 1 changes only in its last step. From the same draw $(x_0,\epsilon)$ and the same $x_t$, $x_0$-prediction minimizes $\lVert x_0-\hat x_0(x_t,t)\rVert^2$, and $v$-prediction computes $v=a_t\epsilon-b_tx_0$ and minimizes $\lVert v-\hat v(x_t,t)\rVert^2$; either output is turned into $\hat x_0$ for the sampler by @eq-v-inverse. An unweighted $\epsilon$-MSE is therefore an SNR-weighted error in $x_0$-space, and an unweighted $v$-MSE is an "SNR+1"-weighted one [@salimans2022, Sec. 4]. As SNR$\to0$ (large $t$), the $\epsilon$-MSE puts almost no weight on the reconstruction error of $x_0$, while the $v$-MSE keeps a weight of at least 1. The three parameterizations are not different generative models but different coordinate systems for the same latent pair; they differ in **how much weight the error at each time receives** (@fig-parameterizations).

![Three prediction targets are one rotation with three loss weightings. (a) In the coefficient plane of $(x_0,\epsilon)$, the noisy input $x_t$ and the velocity $v$ are orthogonal axes turned by the angle $\phi_t$; grey dots mark $(a_t,b_t)$ along the linear schedule and are already bunched near the $\epsilon$ axis for $t\ge500$. (b) The weights that the $\epsilon$-, $x_0$- and $v$-MSE put on the same $x_0$ reconstruction error: $\mathrm{SNR}(t)$, $1$ and $1+\mathrm{SNR}(t)$ (log axis). Definitions and weights of @salimans2022, Sec. 4 and App. D; SNR values from `curves()` in @sec-schedule-code.](figures/lec06/mumbumble-parameterizations.png){#fig-parameterizations width=100%}

**Back to the variational bound.** The same conversion makes the VLB weights of @eq-wt-snr transparent. Multiplying by $\mathrm{SNR}(t)$, which converts an $\epsilon$-error into an $x_0$-error by @eq-parameterization-error-scaling, each interior term is

$$
L_{t-1}
=\frac12\big(\mathrm{SNR}(t-1)-\mathrm{SNR}(t)\big)\,
\mathbb E\lVert x_0-\hat x_0(x_t,t)\rVert^2
\qquad(\sigma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t),
$$ {#eq-vlb-snr}

which is the discrete-time loss of @kingma2021, Sec. 4, Eq. 13. The VLB weights the $x_0$-error at a step by **the SNR lost in that step**, whereas $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}$ weights it by $\mathrm{SNR}(t)$ itself. In $v$-space, by the same identities, the VLB weight is $\tfrac12\big(\mathrm{SNR}(t-1)-\mathrm{SNR}(t)\big)/\big(1+\mathrm{SNR}(t)\big)$. The VLB weights sum to $\tfrac12\big(\mathrm{SNR}(1)-\mathrm{SNR}(T)\big)$, and since the linear schedule loses most of its SNR in the first steps ($\mathrm{SNR}(1)\approx10^4$), most of this total falls on small $t$.

### Training and ancestral sampling {#sec-train-sample}

#### The training algorithm

One training iteration of @eq-simple-loss is [@ho2020, Algorithm 1; @lecture-slides-diffusion, slide 14]:

1. Draw $x_0\sim q_{\mathrm{data}}$.
2. Draw $t\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{1,\ldots,T\}$.
3. Draw the noise $\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$, which is therefore known.
4. Build $x_t$ in one step with @eq-one-step-renoising.
5. Update $\theta$ with $\nabla_\theta\lVert\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\rVert^2$.

Because the noise is drawn by us and added to clean data, the target $\epsilon$ is known exactly and no human labels are needed. Diffusion training is therefore **self-supervised**: the model constructs its own input-target pairs. @fig-self-supervision shows the same clean image corrupted at several noise strengths, with the network estimating the added noise.

![Diffusion training makes its own labels. A synthetic clean image $x_0$, drawn for this chapter from solid-colour shapes, is noised with the one-step renoising formula at three levels of the linear schedule ($t=50,200,500$, so $\bar\alpha_t=0.97,0.66,0.08$), each with its own noise $\epsilon$. A single network $\epsilon_\theta(\cdot,t)$, shared by all noise levels, receives $x_t$ and $t$ and must output the noise that was added.](figures/lec06/mumbumble-self-supervision.png){#fig-self-supervision width=100%}

#### Reverse sampling

After training, draw $x_T\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ and then $x_{t-1}\sim p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ for each $t$ in turn. This samples the joint $p_\theta(x_{0:T})$ in ancestral order; apart from the last step, which reports the mean of $p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)$ instead of a draw from it, the output is a sample of $p_\theta(x_0)$. With @eq-epsilon-parameterization one step is (slides 13--14)

$$
x_{t-1}
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}
\left(
x_t-
\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}
\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)
\right)
+\sigma_t z,
\qquad z\sim\mathcal N(0,I).
$$ {#eq-ddpm-sampling}

In full [@ho2020, Algorithm 2]:

1. Draw $x_T\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$.
2. For $t=T,T-1,\ldots,1$: draw $z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ if $t>1$ and set $z=0$ if $t=1$, then compute $x_{t-1}$ with @eq-ddpm-sampling.
3. Return $x_0$.

The lecture puts the two algorithms side by side and highlights one line in
each (@fig-algorithms). In training it is the argument of $\epsilon_\theta$: the
noisy image is built in a single jump with @eq-one-step-renoising, and no chain
is ever simulated. In sampling it is the bracket: the model mean
$\mu_\theta(x_t,t)$, to which the fresh noise $\sigma_t z$ is then added. Those
two lines are the whole method; everything above derives them.

![The two algorithms of @ho2020 as the lecture presents them (slide 14). Left, training: draw a clean image, a time and a noise vector, build $x_t$ in one jump and take a gradient step on the squared error between $\epsilon$ and $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$. Right, sampling: start from Gaussian noise and apply $T$ reverse steps, each the model mean plus fresh noise of standard deviation $\sigma_t$. The boxed parts are the one-jump construction of $x_t$ and the model mean. From slide 14 of the course slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion], after @ho2020.](figures/lec06/slides-ddpm-algorithms.png){#fig-algorithms width=100%}

Because $1-\alpha_t=\beta_t$, the coefficient in @ho2020, Algorithm 2 is exactly $\beta_t/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$. The final step sets $z=0$: the output is $\mu_\theta(x_1,1)$, the mean of the Gaussian inside the decoder, reported without noise [@ho2020, Sec. 3.3]. Training costs one network evaluation per sampled time, but ancestral sampling needs $T$ sequential evaluations.

@fig-swiss-roll shows the whole procedure on a two-dimensional example, in the spirit of the first figure of @sohl2015 [Sec. 2, Fig. 1]. The forward chain spreads the data into noise, ancestral sampling carries the noise back, and the drift field shows how the reverse mean pulls samples towards the data: diffusion moves **the whole probability mass**, not a single blurred sample.

![Diffusion moves the whole probability mass, not a single sample. Top: forward samples of a Swiss roll at $t=0$, $60$ and $T$. Middle: 600 ancestral DDPM samples ($\sigma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$) recorded at the same times; generation reads this row from right to left. Bottom: the reverse drift $\mu(x_t,t)-x_t$ at $t=1$, $60$ and $T$, rescaled per panel. The reverse process uses the exact score of the empirical law of 1500 Swiss-roll points, so no network is trained, and the samples at $t=0$ land on those training points: the figure shows transport of mass, not generalization. Values from `swiss_roll_figure()` (@sec-swiss-code).](figures/lec06/mumbumble-swiss-roll.png){#fig-swiss-roll width=100%}

#### Why add noise back to the mean?

Why is $\sigma_tz$ added when $\epsilon_\theta$ has already predicted a noise vector? The two quantities play different roles:

- $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ is the network output used to compute the conditional mean $\mu_\theta(x_t,t)$;
- $z$ is a fresh random draw used to sample from the conditional Gaussian $p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ centred at that mean.

DDPM minimizes a KL divergence between the posterior computed from data and a parameterized reverse Gaussian, so both sides are modelled as Gaussian transitions. Sampling from a Gaussian needs the mean plus noise of its standard deviation $\sigma_t$; using the mean alone picks a single point instead of sampling the conditional distribution. Without the injected noise the reverse chain can contract to almost a single point; the numerical example of @sec-experiments shows this. Removing the noise consistently also changes the mean, which is what DDIM does (@sec-ddim).

#### The score, Tweedie's formula and the DDPM mean {#sec-score}

Let $q_t(x_t):=\int q_{\mathrm{data}}(x_0)q(x_t\mid x_0)\,dx_0$ be the marginal at time $t$. Under regularity that allows exchanging differentiation and integration (@sec-proof-tweedie),

$$
\nabla\log q_t(x_t)
=-\frac{\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t]}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}
=-\frac{\epsilon^*(x_t,t)}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}},
\qquad
\mathbb E[x_0\mid x_t]
=\frac{x_t+(1-\bar\alpha_t)\nabla\log q_t(x_t)}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}}.
$$ {#eq-epsilon-score-conversion}

The second identity is **Tweedie's formula**; plugging the optimal predictor into $\hat x_0$ of @eq-epsilon-to-x0 gives exactly this posterior mean. In the same way, writing the DDPM mean @eq-epsilon-parameterization with the score $s_\theta:=-\epsilon_\theta/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$ gives

$$
\mu_\theta(x_t,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t+\beta_t\,s_\theta(x_t,t)\Big),
$$ {#eq-ddpm-mean-score}

which agrees with the mean of the small-step approximation @eq-reverse-small-step to first order in $\beta_t$. Applying Tweedie's formula directly to the one-step model $x_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\epsilon_t$ gives

$$
\mathbb E[x_{t-1}\mid x_t]=\frac{x_t+\beta_t\nabla\log q_t(x_t)}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}
$$ {#eq-one-step-tweedie}

(@sec-proof-tweedie), which is exactly @eq-ddpm-mean-score with the true score. The ideal DDPM mean is therefore the posterior-mean (Tweedie) denoiser for one step, consistent with the minimizer of @eq-mean-matching being $\mathbb E[\tilde\mu_t\mid x_t]=\mathbb E[x_{t-1}\mid x_t]$. Up to time weights, $\epsilon$-prediction MSE is therefore denoising score matching [@vincent2011], the denoising form of the score matching of @hyvarinen2005.

#### Connection to Noise2Score {#sec-tweedie}

Tweedie's formula (@eq-epsilon-score-conversion) connects noise prediction to the score, so one network that estimates the noise, equivalently the score of the noisy data, supplies the information needed for both denoising and generation. Noise2Score [@kim2021] learns that score from noisy images alone and applies Tweedie's formula **once and deterministically** at the noise level of the image. DDPM sampling applies it **iteratively and stochastically** over a sequence of noise levels to create a new sample. Training one noise estimator and reusing it, repeatedly and for several downstream tasks such as denoising and generation, is what slide 14 calls the pattern of foundation models: pretraining followed by (iterative) downstream tasks.

## DDIM: a non-Markovian forward process and deterministic sampling {#sec-ddim}

DDIM, the subject of slides 17--25, changes the latent inference path while retaining the same family of noisy marginals [@ddim]. Because those marginals determine the denoising inputs, the same noise-prediction network can be reused, under assumptions made precise below. This freedom yields a deterministic sampler and permits generation on a shorter subsequence of times. Slide 17 and the original DDIM paper write DDPM's $\bar\alpha_t$ as $\alpha_t$; all equations below use the notation of this chapter [@ddim].

### Motivation: is the Markov property needed?

DDPM specifies a Markov forward path and models its small reverse steps with Gaussian transitions. DDIM observes that the simplified loss @eq-simple-loss depends on the forward process only through the noisy marginals $q(x_t\mid x_0)$, not through the coupling between different times. It therefore constructs a broader inference family in which a transition can depend directly on the clean endpoint $x_0$. The blue dashed arrows in @fig-ddim-graph (b) show this dependence. The generative update (@eq-ddim-step) still depends on the current state $x_t$ and fresh noise only, so the generative process is Markov; the **forward inference distribution** $q_\gamma$ is the non-Markovian object.

![DDIM keeps the marginals and changes only the inference path. (a) In DDPM each forward transition $q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})$ (grey dashed) depends only on the previous state. (b) In DDIM each forward transition $q_\gamma(x_t\mid x_{t-1},x_0)$ also conditions on the clean $x_0$ (blue dashed). Both models share the generative chain $p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ from $x_3$ to $x_0$ (solid) and the marginals $q(x_t\mid x_0)$.](figures/lec06/mumbumble-ddim-graph.png){#fig-ddim-graph width=100%}

### The non-Markovian forward family

For each sequence $\gamma=(\gamma_2,\ldots,\gamma_T)$ with $0\le\gamma_t^2\le1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}$, define the family of slides 19--21 [@ddim, Sec. 3.1, Eqs. 6--7]

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_\gamma(x_T\mid x_0)&=\mathcal N\!\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_T}x_0,(1-\bar\alpha_T)I\right),\\
q_\gamma(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)&=q_\gamma(x_T\mid x_0)\prod_{t=2}^{T}q_\gamma(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0),
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
q_\gamma(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)
=\mathcal N\!\left(
\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,x_0
+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\gamma_t^2}\;
\frac{x_t-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}},\;
\gamma_t^2I
\right).
$$ {#eq-ddim-posterior}

The family is built so that the DDPM marginals survive.

::: {#prp-ddim-marginal}
## Marginal preservation
The family @eq-ddim-posterior has the same marginals as DDPM for every $t=1,\ldots,T$: $q_\gamma(x_t\mid x_0)=\mathcal N(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0,(1-\bar\alpha_t)I)$. Slide 20 states the result.
:::

*Proof.* By backward induction from $t=T$ [@ddim, App. B, Lemma 1]. At $t=T$ the claim is the definition. If it holds at $t$, write $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$ with $\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ and draw $x_{t-1}$ from @eq-ddim-posterior with a fresh $z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$. Since $(x_t-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0)/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}=\epsilon$,

$$
x_{t-1}=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\gamma_t^2}\;\epsilon+\gamma_tz,
$$

and since $\epsilon$ and $z$ are independent, @lem-gauss-lin gives the mean $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0$ and the covariance $\big[(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\gamma_t^2)+\gamma_t^2\big]I=(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})I$. $\square$

The coefficient $\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\gamma_t^2}$ is essential: with $\bar\alpha_t$ in place of $\bar\alpha_{t-1}$ the covariance would be $(1-\bar\alpha_t)I$ and the induction would break.

With the marginals in hand, the forward-time conditional follows from Bayes' rule (slide 19):

$$
q_\gamma(x_t\mid x_{t-1},x_0)
=q_\gamma(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\,\frac{q_\gamma(x_t\mid x_0)}{q_\gamma(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)}.
$$

All three factors are Gaussian, so this conditional can be written out. Given $x_0$, write $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$ and draw $x_{t-1}$ from @eq-ddim-posterior as $x_{t-1}=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\gamma_t^2}\,\epsilon+\gamma_tz$. The pair is jointly Gaussian with $\mathrm{Cov}(x_t,x_{t-1}\mid x_0)=\sqrt{(1-\bar\alpha_t)(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\gamma_t^2)}\,I$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)=(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})I$, and conditioning on $x_{t-1}$ gives, for $\gamma_t>0$,

$$
q_\gamma(x_t\mid x_{t-1},x_0)
=\mathcal N\!\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\frac{\sqrt{(1-\bar\alpha_t)(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\gamma_t^2)}}{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\big(x_{t-1}-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,x_0\big),\;\frac{(1-\bar\alpha_t)\,\gamma_t^2}{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,I\right).
$$ {#eq-ddim-forward}

For $\gamma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$ the coefficient of $x_{t-1}$ is $\sqrt{\alpha_t}$, the $x_0$ terms cancel because $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}=\sqrt{\alpha_t}\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}$, and the variance is $\beta_t$, so @eq-ddim-forward reduces to the DDPM transition @eq-forward-chain. For any other $\gamma_t$ this transition depends on the clean image $x_0$ as well as on the previous state, so the inference path is not Markov, although its marginals are those of DDPM.

Because the marginals are the same, DDIM uses the same one-step renoising inputs as @eq-one-step-renoising. The relation between its variational objective and the simplified loss is derived below. The DDIM posterior mean should not be identified with the DDPM mean $\tilde\mu_t$ in general; the two coincide only for the variance choice $\gamma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$ proved in @prp-ddim-ddpm.

### The generative step

At generation time $x_0$ is unknown, so the prediction $\hat x_0=(x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t))/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$ of @eq-epsilon-to-x0 is substituted for $x_0$ in @eq-ddim-posterior (slides 21--22). Then $(x_t-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\hat x_0)/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}=\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ exactly, so one step is

$$
x_{t-1}
=\underbrace{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\;\frac{x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}}}_{\text{predicted }x_0}
+\underbrace{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\gamma_t^2}\;\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)}_{\text{direction pointing to }x_t}
+\underbrace{\gamma_t\,z}_{\text{random noise}}.
$$ {#eq-ddim-step}

This is the update of slide 17, @ddim, Sec. 4.1, Eq. 12, in the notation of this chapter. Comparing it with @eq-ddpm-sampling shows that both the fresh-noise coefficient and the deterministic mean direction depend on $\gamma_t$.

### The exact relation to DDPM and deterministic sampling {#sec-ddim-exact}

Writing both samplers in the same coordinates makes their relation exact.

::: {#prp-ddim-ddpm}
## Reduction to DDPM
With $\gamma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$, @eq-ddim-posterior equals the DDPM posterior $\mathcal N(\tilde\mu_t,\tilde\beta_tI)$. The DDPM ancestral step @eq-ddpm-sampling ($\sigma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$) can therefore be written

$$
x_{t-1}^{\mathrm{DDPM}}
=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\hat x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\tilde\beta_t}\;\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)+\sqrt{\tilde\beta_t}\,z.
$$ {#eq-ddpm-in-ddim-form}

Proof in @sec-proof-ddim-ddpm.
:::

Deterministic DDIM ($\gamma_t=0$), on the other hand, is

$$
x_{t-1}^{\mathrm{DDIM}}
=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\hat x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\;\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t).
$$ {#eq-ddim-deterministic}

The two differ in exactly two places. (i) The variance $\tilde\beta_t$ that DDPM injects as fresh noise is carried deterministically by DDIM along the predicted noise direction $\epsilon_\theta$, so the coefficient of the "direction pointing to $x_t$" grows from $\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\tilde\beta_t}$ to $\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}$. (ii) There is no $z$ term. Seen in the original DDPM form @eq-ddpm-sampling, this is why the mean looks different and there seems to be an extra $\epsilon_\theta$ term.

Intermediate choices are parameterized as $\gamma_t=\eta\sqrt{\tilde\beta_t}$, with $\eta=1$ giving DDPM and $\eta=0$ giving DDIM [@ddim, Sec. 5, Eq. 16]. With $\gamma_t=0$ the whole path down to $x_0$ is fixed as soon as $x_T$ is fixed, so DDIM is an implicit probabilistic model; the initial $x_T$ is still drawn at random.

#### Denoise, then re-noise {#sec-denoise-renoise}

The three terms of @eq-ddim-step were named after @ddim, which is how they are
usually quoted. The lecture renames them, and the renaming is the point of the
slide (slide 23):

$$
x_{t-1}
=\underbrace{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\hat x_0(x_t,t)}_{\text{Tweedie's denoiser}}
+\underbrace{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\gamma_t^2}\;\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)}_{\text{parametric noise}}
+\underbrace{\gamma_t\,z}_{\text{stochastic noise}} .
$$ {#eq-denoise-renoise}

The first term is not merely a prediction of $x_0$: by @eq-epsilon-score-conversion
it is the Tweedie denoiser of @sec-tweedie applied at noise level $t$ --- the
same @thm-tweedie that the previous chapter derived for self-supervised
denoising. What the second
and third terms do is put the sample back at the noise level $t-1$, splitting
that re-noising between a direction the network computes and a draw that it
does not. Every sampler in this chapter is one denoising step followed by one
re-noising step, and $\eta$ decides only how much of the re-noising is random.

This also explains why the noise cannot simply be dropped from DDPM while the
mean is kept. The marginal of $x_{t-1}$ has to carry variance
$1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}$; take away the $\gamma_t z$ term and the coefficient of
$\epsilon_\theta$ must grow to make up the difference, which is exactly
@eq-ddim-deterministic. The lecture draws this as a sequence of manifolds
$\mathcal{M}_t$, one per noise level, with each step dropping to the data
manifold and climbing back to the next one up (slide 24). Keeping that
transition on the right manifold is what the later chapters return to.

### Why the same network serves every variance choice {#sec-ddim-objective}

The common noise-prediction objective follows from Theorem 1 of @ddim [Sec. 3.2]. Because $q_\gamma(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)$ is defined directly in reverse order, its variational bound splits into KL terms like @eq-vlb-decomposition without the Bayes rearrangement @eq-bayes-rearrange. In each interior term both Gaussians have covariance $\gamma_t^2I$, and their means differ only through $x_0$ versus $\hat x_0$. Let $c_t$ be the coefficient of $x_0$ in the mean of @eq-ddim-posterior,

$$
c_t:=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\gamma_t^2}\,\sqrt{\frac{\bar\alpha_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}}>0 .
$$

Then each interior term is a weighted noise-prediction error,

$$
\mathbb E_q\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_\gamma(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\,\Vert\,p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\right)\right]
=\lambda_t\,\mathbb E\lVert\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\rVert^2,
\qquad
\lambda_t=\frac{c_t^2}{2\gamma_t^2\,\mathrm{SNR}(t)},
$$ {#eq-ddim-weights}

for every $\gamma_t>0$ (@sec-proof-ddim-objective). Here $p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ is the generative step (@eq-ddim-step), and by @prp-ddim-marginal the expectation runs over the same pairs $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon$ as $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}$. For $\gamma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$, $\lambda_t$ reduces to $w_t$ of @eq-wt-simplified, as it must.

Since every $\lambda_t$ is positive, @eq-bayes-optimal applies. **If** $\epsilon_\theta(\cdot,t)$ can represent any function of $x_t$ for each $t$, the idealization of @sec-proof-bayes, then all these objectives and $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}$ have the same minimizer $\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t]$. In this sense the network trained for DDPM can be used for any $\gamma$ without retraining. A finite network shared across $t$ only approximates this common minimizer. The deterministic case $\gamma_t=0$ is not covered by this identity, since $\lambda_t\to\infty$ as $\gamma_t\to0$. @ddim [Sec. 4.1] introduce it as the special case $\gamma_t=0$ of the generative process and note that, although their Theorem 1 does not cover it, it can be approximated by making $\gamma_t$ very small; every such $\gamma$ shares the minimizer above.

### Skipping steps {#sec-skip}

Choose a subsequence $1=\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_S=T$ and write @eq-ddim-posterior for each consecutive pair $s=\tau_{i-1}<t=\tau_i$, with $\bar\alpha_s$ in place of $\bar\alpha_{t-1}$. The proof of @prp-ddim-marginal uses only the marginals at the two times involved, so every selected time keeps its marginal; @ddim attach the unselected times directly to $x_0$ through $q(x_t\mid x_0)$, which keeps the bound valid and plays no role in sampling [App. C.1]. A model trained with $T=1000$ can therefore sample in $S\ll T$ steps [@ddim, Sec. 4.2]. For $\eta=1$ the variance is the posterior variance of the jump: @prp-posterior with $\beta_t$ replaced by the variance $1-\bar\alpha_t/\bar\alpha_s$ of the forward transition from $s$ to $t$, and $\bar\alpha_{t-1}$ by $\bar\alpha_s$. The marginals remain exact for large jumps, but errors in $\hat x_0$ and discretization errors grow with the jump (@sec-experiments). Deterministic sampling tolerates large jumps best: with 20 to 100 steps DDIM gives samples comparable to 1000-step models, a 10 to 50 times speed-up [@ddim, Sec. 5.1]. In full, generalized DDIM sampling on a subsequence is:

1. Choose $1=\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_S=T$ and $\eta\in[0,1]$, and draw $x_{\tau_S}\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$.
2. For $i=S,\ldots,1$, with $t=\tau_i$, $s=\tau_{i-1}$ and $\tau_0:=0$: compute $\hat\epsilon=\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ and $\hat x_0$ by @eq-epsilon-to-x0, set $\gamma^2=\eta^2\frac{1-\bar\alpha_s}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\big(1-\frac{\bar\alpha_t}{\bar\alpha_s}\big)$, and update $x_s=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_s}\,\hat x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_s-\gamma^2}\,\hat\epsilon+\gamma z$ with a fresh $z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$.
3. Return $x_0$. At the last step $\bar\alpha_0=1$ gives $\gamma=0$ and $x_0=\hat x_0$, the counterpart of reporting the decoder mean in DDPM.

The function `ddim` in @sec-experiments implements exactly these steps.

### DDPM and DDIM side by side

@tbl-ddpm-ddim collects the differences between the two samplers.

| | DDPM | DDIM |
|---|---|---|
| Forward structure | Markov chain linking adjacent states only | non-Markovian family $q_\gamma$ that may depend on $x_0$ |
| Marginal at each time | @eq-forward-marginal | same as DDPM (@prp-ddim-marginal) |
| Training | $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ trained with @eq-simple-loss | the same $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ reused |
| One step | @eq-ddpm-sampling | @eq-ddim-step; with $\gamma_t=0$, @eq-ddim-deterministic |
| Stochasticity | fresh noise at every step | controlled by $\eta\in[0,1]$; deterministic for $\eta=0$ |
| Number of steps | all $T$ training steps in @ho2020; on a subsequence it is DDIM with $\eta=1$ | any subsequence of $S\le T$ steps |

: DDPM and DDIM compared. The last two rows draw on @sec-ddim-exact and @sec-skip. {#tbl-ddpm-ddim}

## Reproducible numerical examples {#sec-experiments}

The following computations check the equations numerically and isolate the difference between the DDPM and DDIM samplers using the Bayes-optimal noise predictor. All code uses only the Python standard library, except the Swiss-roll snippet of @sec-swiss-code, which uses NumPy. The plotted figures are drawn with TikZ directly from the values these functions return; the drawing code only places those values on axes.

### A two-step scalar example

Fix two steps with $x_0=2$, $(\beta_1,\beta_2)=(0.1,0.2)$ and $(\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)=(0.5,-1)$. Then $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\bar\alpha_2)=(0.9,0.8,0.72)$, and the forward samples are

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_1&=\sqrt{0.9}(2)+\sqrt{0.1}(0.5)\approx2.0555,\\
x_2&=\sqrt{0.8}(2.0555)+\sqrt{0.2}(-1)\approx1.3913,\\
\epsilon
&=\frac{x_2-\sqrt{0.72}x_0}{\sqrt{0.28}}
\approx-0.5779.
\end{aligned}
$$

The variance of the two-step noise is $\alpha_2\beta_1+\beta_2=0.28=1-\bar\alpha_2$, so the last line is the noise that expresses the same $x_2$ in one step through @eq-one-step-renoising. Substituting the same numbers into @eq-posterior-mean,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tilde\beta_2
&=\frac{1-0.9}{1-0.72}(0.2)
=\frac1{14}\approx0.07143,\\
\tilde\mu_2(x_2,x_0)
&=\frac{\sqrt{0.8}(1-0.9)(1.3913)+0.2\sqrt{0.9}(2)}{1-0.72}
\approx1.7997.
\end{aligned}
$$

The actual $x_1=2.0555$ on this path lies about $0.96$ standard deviations above the posterior mean: the posterior mean is the centre of the conditional distribution, not the latent that happened to be drawn.

Assume an oracle predictor that returns exactly the noise of this path, $\epsilon_\theta(x_2,2)=\epsilon=-0.5779$. Then @eq-epsilon-to-x0 returns $\hat x_0=2$ exactly, and three updates can be compared:

- @eq-posterior-mean-epsilon (the DDPM mean): $\frac{1}{\sqrt{0.8}}\big(1.3913-\frac{0.2}{\sqrt{0.28}}(-0.5779)\big)\approx1.7997$, equal to $\tilde\mu_2$.
- @eq-ddim-step with $\gamma_2^2=\tilde\beta_2$: $\sqrt{0.9}(2)+\sqrt{0.1-0.07143}(-0.5779)\approx1.7997$, equal to the DDPM mean as @prp-ddim-ddpm says.
- Deterministic DDIM ($\gamma_2=0$): $\sqrt{0.9}(2)+\sqrt{0.1}(-0.5779)\approx1.7146$. Instead of adding fresh noise, it moves further along the $\epsilon$ direction.

```{.python}
import math
sq = math.sqrt
x0, b1, b2, e1, e2 = 2.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, -1.0
a1, a2 = 1 - b1, 1 - b2
ab1, ab2 = a1, a1 * a2
x1 = sq(a1) * x0 + sq(b1) * e1                    # forward step 1
x2 = sq(a2) * x1 + sq(b2) * e2                    # forward step 2
eps = (x2 - sq(ab2) * x0) / sq(1 - ab2)           # one-step noise
bt = (1 - ab1) / (1 - ab2) * b2                   # beta_tilde_2
mu = (sq(a2) * (1 - ab1) * x2 + b2 * sq(ab1) * x0) / (1 - ab2)
mu_eps = (x2 - b2 / sq(1 - ab2) * eps) / sq(a2)   # epsilon form
x0_hat = (x2 - sq(1 - ab2) * eps) / sq(ab2)       # exact eps given
ddim0 = sq(ab1) * x0_hat + sq(1 - ab1) * eps      # gamma = 0
ddimb = sq(ab1) * x0_hat + sq(1 - ab1 - bt) * eps  # gamma^2 = bt
z = (x1 - mu) / sq(bt)
print(f"x1={x1:.4f} x2={x2:.4f} eps={eps:.4f} beta_tilde={bt:.5f}")
print(f"mu={mu:.4f} mu_eps={mu_eps:.4f} z={z:.3f}")
print(f"x0_hat={x0_hat:.4f} ddim0={ddim0:.4f} ddim_bt={ddimb:.4f}")
# x1=2.0555 x2=1.3913 eps=-0.5779 beta_tilde=0.07143
# mu=1.7997 mu_eps=1.7997 z=0.957
# x0_hat=2.0000 ddim0=1.7146 ddim_bt=1.7997
```

### DDPM and DDIM on a one-dimensional mixture

Using the Bayes-optimal noise predictor $\epsilon^*(x_t,t)=\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t]$ (@eq-bayes-optimal), computed analytically, instead of a trained network isolates the properties of the samplers from training error. Note that this is the conditional mean of the noise, not the noise actually added on a path. Take the data to be the one-dimensional Gaussian mixture $x_0\sim0.3\,\mathcal N(-1.5,0.2^2)+0.7\,\mathcal N(1,0.3^2)$. Blurring each component with @eq-forward-marginal gives $q_t(x)=\sum_k\pi_k\mathcal N(x;\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\mu_k,V_{t,k})$ with $V_{t,k}=\bar\alpha_ts_k^2+1-\bar\alpha_t$. With the responsibilities $r_k(x)=\pi_k\mathcal N(x;\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\mu_k,V_{t,k})/q_t(x)$, @eq-epsilon-score-conversion gives

$$
\epsilon^*(x,t)=-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\nabla\log q_t(x)=\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\sum_kr_k(x)\frac{x-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\mu_k}{V_{t,k}}.
$$

With the linear schedule ($T=1000$), $N=4000$ draws $x_T\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ were run through 1000-step DDPM ($\sigma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$) and through deterministic DDIM on an evenly spaced subsequence of $S$ steps. @tbl-mixture reports the fraction $P$ in the right mode and the mean / standard deviation of each mode (boundary $x=-0.25$).

| Sampler | Steps $S$ | $P(\text{right})$ | Left mode | Right mode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Target | --- | 0.700 | $-1.500$ / 0.200 | $+1.000$ / 0.300 |
| DDPM | 1000 | 0.706 | $-1.487$ / 0.200 | $+1.003$ / 0.293 |
| DDIM, $\eta=0$ | 50 | 0.701 | $-1.479$ / 0.191 | $+0.991$ / 0.286 |
| DDIM, $\eta=0$ | 10 | 0.721 | $-1.404$ / 0.230 | $+0.932$ / 0.263 |

: Final samples on the one-dimensional mixture with the Bayes-optimal predictor ($N=4000$). Each mode entry is mean / standard deviation. {#tbl-mixture}

With $N=4000$ the standard error of $P$ is about 0.007. Three observations follow.

1. **Both samplers closely approximate the same target.** With $\epsilon^*$, 1000-step DDPM and 50-step deterministic DDIM ($\eta=0$) reproduce the target mode fraction to within one standard error, and the mode means and standard deviations to within $0.021$ (@fig-ddpm-vs-ddim (c)). The remaining discrepancies come from the Gaussian reverse-transition approximation in finite-step DDPM, the discretization error of finite-step DDIM, the small mismatch between $q_T$ and $\mathcal N(0,I)$, and Monte Carlo error. The experiment therefore supports reuse of the same ideal noise predictor without claiming that either finite-step sampler is exact.
2. **DDIM is deterministic.** Started twice from the same $x_T=0.3$, DDIM returns $0.9608$ both times, while DDPM returns different values each time, here $-1.4437$ and $1.3192$, in different modes. In @fig-ddpm-vs-ddim (a)--(b), DDPM paths jitter at every step and can reach different modes from the same start, while DDIM paths are smooth and, for these 50 steps, keep the order of their starting points.
3. **Too few steps fail.** At $S=10$ deterministic DDIM errs clearly: the right-mode fraction is $0.721$ against $0.700$, the left-mode mean $-1.404$ against $-1.500$, and the left-mode spread $0.230$ against $0.200$. The inference family keeps exact marginals on any subsequence (@sec-skip), but the generative chain substitutes $\hat x_0$ for $x_0$, and the resulting error grows with the size of each jump.

**Dropping the noise of DDPM.** Running the DDPM mean with $z=0$ at every step, from the first 400 of the same draws $x_T$, sends every sample to $x_0\in[0.955,0.965]$: without the injected noise the chain here contracts to almost a single point near the larger mode, which is why the sampler of @sec-train-sample adds $\sigma_tz$.

![One noise predictor, two samplers, the same target. With the Bayes-optimal predictor $\epsilon^*$ on the mixture of @tbl-mixture: (a) eight paths of 1000-step DDPM jitter because fresh noise enters at every step; (b) 50-step deterministic DDIM paths from the same eight starts are smooth, with dots where $\epsilon^*$ is evaluated; (c) histograms (45 bins on $[-2.5,2]$) of the $N=4000$ final samples of both samplers match the true density (grey). Grey horizontal lines in (a) and (b) mark the mode means $-1.5$ and $1$, and generation runs from left to right. All plotted values are returned by `figure_data()` in the code below.](figures/lec06/mumbumble-ddpm-vs-ddim.png){#fig-ddpm-vs-ddim width=100%}

The following code reproduces @tbl-mixture, the determinism check, the $z=0$ experiment and panel (b) of @fig-variance-vlb exactly (about 20 seconds with CPython 3.12); its output is listed in the final comments, and `figure_data()` returns the paths and histograms of @fig-ddpm-vs-ddim.

```{.python}
import math, random

T = 1000
# beta[t-1] = beta_t, linear from 1e-4 to 0.02
beta = [1e-4 + (0.02 - 1e-4) * i / (T - 1) for i in range(T)]
abar = [1.0]                                  # abar[t], abar[0] = 1
for b in beta:
    abar.append(abar[-1] * (1 - b))

# data: 0.3 N(-1.5, 0.2^2) + 0.7 N(1, 0.3^2)
PI, MU, SD = (0.3, 0.7), (-1.5, 1.0), (0.2, 0.3)

def eps_star(x, t):
    """Exact E[eps | x_t = x] = -sqrt(1 - abar_t) * score."""
    a, logw, z = abar[t], [], []
    for p, m, s in zip(PI, MU, SD):
        var = a * s * s + 1 - a           # Var(x_t | component)
        d = x - math.sqrt(a) * m
        lp = math.log(p) - 0.5 * math.log(var) - d * d / (2 * var)
        logw.append(lp)
        z.append(d / var)
    w = [math.exp(l - max(logw)) for l in logw]
    num = sum(wi * zi for wi, zi in zip(w, z))
    return math.sqrt(1 - a) * num / sum(w)

def ddpm(x, rng, path=None):
    """Ancestral sampling with sigma_t^2 = beta_tilde_t."""
    for t in range(T, 0, -1):
        b = beta[t - 1]
        e = eps_star(x, t)
        mean = (x - b / math.sqrt(1 - abar[t]) * e)
        mean /= math.sqrt(1 - b)
        var = (1 - abar[t - 1]) / (1 - abar[t]) * b
        if t > 1:                             # z = 0 at t = 1
            mean += math.sqrt(var) * rng.gauss(0, 1)
        x = mean
        if path is not None: path.append((t - 1, x))
    return x

def ddim(x, steps=50, eta=0.0, rng=None, path=None):
    """Generalized DDIM on an evenly spaced sub-sequence of 1..T."""
    taus = [round(1 + i * (T - 1) / (steps - 1))
            for i in range(steps)]
    for i in range(steps - 1, -1, -1):
        t, s = taus[i], (taus[i - 1] if i > 0 else 0)
        e = eps_star(x, t)
        x0_hat = (x - math.sqrt(1 - abar[t]) * e)
        x0_hat /= math.sqrt(abar[t])
        r = 1 - abar[t] / abar[s]
        g2 = eta ** 2 * (1 - abar[s]) / (1 - abar[t]) * r
        k = math.sqrt(1 - abar[s] - g2)
        x = math.sqrt(abar[s]) * x0_hat + k * e
        if g2 > 0: x += math.sqrt(g2) * rng.gauss(0, 1)
        if path is not None: path.append((s, x))
    return x

def summary(xs):
    def ms(xs):
        m = sum(xs) / len(xs)
        return m, math.sqrt(sum((u - m) ** 2 for u in xs) / len(xs))
    L = [u for u in xs if u <= -0.25]
    R = [u for u in xs if u > -0.25]
    return len(R) / len(xs), ms(L), ms(R)

def report(name, xs):
    p, (mL, sL), (mR, sR) = summary(xs)
    print(f"{name:13s} P={p:.3f}  L {mL:+.3f}/{sL:.3f}"
          f"  R {mR:+.3f}/{sR:.3f}")

def figure_data():
    """Paths and histograms drawn in the figure."""
    starts = [-1.6, -0.9, -0.35, 0.05, 0.3, 0.75, 1.3, 1.9]
    prng, paths_ddpm, paths_ddim = random.Random(7), [], []
    for x in starts:
        p = [(T, x)]
        ddpm(x, prng, p)
        paths_ddpm.append(p[::8] + [p[-1]])  # every 8th step
        q = [(T, x)]
        ddim(x, 50, path=q)
        paths_ddim.append(q)
    rng = random.Random(0)
    xT = [rng.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(4000)]
    s_ddpm = [ddpm(x, rng) for x in xT]   # same draws as the table
    s_ddim = [ddim(x, 50) for x in xT]
    lo, hi, nb = -2.5, 2.0, 45
    def hist(xs):                          # density per bin
        cnt = [0] * nb
        for x in xs:
            i = int((x - lo) / (hi - lo) * nb)
            if 0 <= i < nb: cnt[i] += 1
        return [n / (len(xs) * (hi - lo) / nb) for n in cnt]
    return paths_ddpm, paths_ddim, hist(s_ddpm), hist(s_ddim)

def vlb_terms(n=1401):
    """Interior VLB terms L_{t-1} (nats), t = 2..T, with eps*."""
    h, out = 14 / (n - 1), []
    for t in range(2, T + 1):
        a, e2 = abar[t], 0.0
        for i in range(n):
            x = -7 + i * h
            q = sum(p * math.exp(-(x - math.sqrt(a) * m) ** 2
                                 / (2 * (a * s * s + 1 - a)))
                    / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi * (a * s * s + 1 - a))
                    for p, m, s in zip(PI, MU, SD))
            e2 += q * eps_star(x, t) ** 2 * h
        b = beta[t - 1]
        out.append(b / (2 * (1 - b) * (1 - abar[t - 1])) * (1 - e2))
    return out

def ddpm_mean_only(x):
    """DDPM with the noise term dropped: z = 0 at every step."""
    for t in range(T, 0, -1):
        b = beta[t - 1]
        e = eps_star(x, t)
        x = (x - b / math.sqrt(1 - abar[t]) * e) / math.sqrt(1 - b)
    return x

if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng, N = random.Random(0), 4000
    xT = [rng.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(N)]
    print("target        P=0.700  L -1.500/0.200  R +1.000/0.300")
    report("DDPM, T=1000", [ddpm(x, rng) for x in xT])
    for steps in (50, 10):
        report(f"DDIM, S={steps}", [ddim(x, steps) for x in xT])
    d1, d2 = ddim(0.3), ddim(0.3)
    p1, p2 = ddpm(0.3, rng), ddpm(0.3, rng)
    print("x_T = 0.3: DDIM", round(d1, 4), round(d2, 4),
          "| DDPM", round(p1, 4), round(p2, 4))
    zs = [ddpm_mean_only(x) for x in xT[:400]]
    print("z = 0 throughout: x_0 in [%.3f, %.3f]"
          % (min(zs), max(zs)))
    L = vlb_terms()
    print("VLB terms: L_1 %.2f, L_999 %.1e" % (L[0], L[998]),
          "| share of t<=10: %.1f%%" % (100 * sum(L[:9]) / sum(L)))
# target        P=0.700  L -1.500/0.200  R +1.000/0.300
# DDPM, T=1000  P=0.706  L -1.487/0.200  R +1.003/0.293
# DDIM, S=50    P=0.701  L -1.479/0.191  R +0.991/0.286
# DDIM, S=10    P=0.721  L -1.404/0.230  R +0.932/0.263
# x_T = 0.3: DDIM 0.9608 0.9608 | DDPM -1.4437 1.3192
# z = 0 throughout: x_0 in [0.955, 0.965]
# VLB terms: L_1 0.60, L_999 5.7e-07 | share of t<=10: 42.6%
```

### The Swiss roll {#sec-swiss-code}

@fig-swiss-roll uses the exact score of an empirical distribution: with data points $d_1,\ldots,d_n$, the noisy marginal $q_t$ is a mixture of Gaussians centred at $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}d_i$, and $\epsilon^*$ follows from @eq-epsilon-score-conversion as a softmax-weighted average. The following NumPy code returns the plotted points and arrows (about 40 seconds). Its check, listed in the final comment, confirms the caption: the median distance from a generated sample at $t=0$ to the nearest training point is 0.0045, far below the 0.03 jitter of the data.

```{.python}
import math
import numpy as np

T = 1000
beta = np.linspace(1e-4, 0.02, T)
abar = np.concatenate([[1.0], np.cumprod(1 - beta)])

def roll(n, rng):
    th = 1.5 * np.pi + 3 * np.pi * rng.random(n)
    p = np.stack([th * np.cos(th), th * np.sin(th)], 1) / 6
    return p + 0.03 * rng.standard_normal(p.shape)

data = roll(1500, np.random.default_rng(0))   # empirical law

def eps_star(x, t):
    """E[eps | x_t = x] under the empirical data law."""
    a, b2 = math.sqrt(abar[t]), 1 - abar[t]
    d2 = ((x[:, None] - a * data[None]) ** 2).sum(-1)
    w = np.exp(-(d2 - d2.min(1, keepdims=True)) / (2 * b2))
    w /= w.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    return (x - a * w @ data) / math.sqrt(b2)

def mean(x, t):                                # DDPM reverse mean
    e = eps_star(x, t)
    return (x - beta[t - 1] / math.sqrt(1 - abar[t]) * e) \
        / math.sqrt(1 - beta[t - 1])

def swiss_roll_figure(times=(0, 60, T)):
    """Forward samples, reverse samples and drift field."""
    x0 = roll(600, np.random.default_rng(1))
    z = np.random.default_rng(2).standard_normal(x0.shape)
    fwd = {t: math.sqrt(abar[t]) * x0 + math.sqrt(1 - abar[t]) * z
           for t in times}
    g = np.random.default_rng(3)
    x = g.standard_normal((600, 2))
    rev = {T: x.copy()}
    for t in range(T, 0, -1):
        var = (1 - abar[t - 1]) / (1 - abar[t]) * beta[t - 1]
        x = mean(x, t)
        if t > 1:
            x = x + math.sqrt(var) * g.standard_normal(x.shape)
        if t - 1 in times:
            rev[t - 1] = x.copy()
    s = np.linspace(-2.4, 2.4, 13)
    grid = np.stack(np.meshgrid(s, s), -1).reshape(-1, 2)
    drift = {t: mean(grid, max(t, 1)) - grid for t in times}
    return fwd, rev, drift

if __name__ == "__main__":
    fwd, rev, drift = swiss_roll_figure()
    d = np.sqrt(((rev[0][:, None] - data[None]) ** 2).sum(-1))
    print("t=0 samples: median distance to nearest data point",
          round(float(np.median(d.min(1))), 4))
# t=0 samples: median distance to nearest data point 0.0045
```

### Schedule and weight statistics {#sec-schedule-code}

The schedule and weight values quoted in @sec-schedule (including the cosine schedule), @sec-small-step, @sec-vlb-terms and @tbl-vlb-weights are reproduced by the following code, whose output is listed in the final comments; `curves()` returns the curves plotted in @fig-noise-schedule, @fig-parameterizations (b) and @fig-variance-vlb (a).

```{.python}
import math

T = 1000
beta = [1e-4 + (0.02 - 1e-4) * i / (T - 1) for i in range(T)]
abar = [1.0]
for b in beta:
    abar.append(abar[-1] * (1 - b))

def snr(t):
    return abar[t] / (1 - abar[t])

def ratio(t):           # beta_t / (alpha_t (1 - abar_{t-1}))
    return beta[t - 1] / ((1 - beta[t - 1]) * (1 - abar[t - 1]))

def curves(TT=1000):
    """beta_t, abar_t, SNR(t) and tilde-beta_t / beta_t of the
    linear schedule shortened to TT steps (ends times 1000/TT)."""
    sc = 1000 / TT
    b = [sc * (1e-4 + (0.02 - 1e-4) * i / (TT - 1))
         for i in range(TT)]
    ab = [1.0]
    for x in b:
        ab.append(ab[-1] * (1 - x))
    snr_t = [ab[t] / (1 - ab[t]) for t in range(1, TT + 1)]
    ratio_t = [(1 - ab[t - 1]) / (1 - ab[t])
               for t in range(1, TT + 1)]
    return b, ab, snr_t, ratio_t

def cosine_abar(t, s=0.008):   # Nichol & Dhariwal, Sec. 3.2
    f = lambda u: math.cos((u / T + s) / (1 + s) * math.pi / 2) ** 2
    return f(t) / f(0)

half = min(range(1, T + 1), key=lambda t: abs(abar[t] - 0.5))
print("abar_t closest to 1/2 at t =", half,
      "| abar_T =", f"{abar[T]:.1e}")
print("cosine: abar_t closest to 1/2 at t =",
      min(range(1, T + 1), key=lambda t: abs(cosine_abar(t) - 0.5)))
print("SNR(1) =", f"{snr(1):.0f}", "| SNR(T) =", f"{snr(T):.1e}")
print("L_T/d bound:", f"{-0.5 * math.log(1 - abar[T]):.1e} nats")
print("ratio at t = 2:", round(ratio(2), 2))
ts = range(2, T + 1)    # interior terms t = 2..T
w = {"tilde": [ratio(t) / 2 for t in ts],
     "beta": [beta[t - 1] / (2 * (1 - beta[t - 1]) * (1 - abar[t]))
              for t in ts],
     "simple": [1.0 for t in ts]}
for k, vals in w.items():
    m, tot = sum(vals) / len(vals), sum(vals)
    rel = [round(vals[t - 2] / m, 2) for t in (2, 10, 100, 500)]
    print(f"{k:6s}", rel, f"t<=10 {sum(vals[:9]) / tot:.1%}",
          f"t<=100 {sum(vals[:99]) / tot:.1%}")
x = [math.log(t) for t in range(2, 101)]
y = [math.log(w["tilde"][t - 2]) for t in range(2, 101)]
mx, my = sum(x) / len(x), sum(y) / len(y)
num = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(x, y))
print("log-log slope, t = 2..100:",
      round(num / sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in x), 2))
# abar_t closest to 1/2 at t = 259 | abar_T = 4.0e-05
# cosine: abar_t closest to 1/2 at t = 496
# SNR(1) = 9999 | SNR(T) = 4.0e-05
# L_T/d bound: 2.0e-05 nats
# ratio at t = 2: 1.2
# tilde  [58.9, 8.49, 1.01, 0.54] t<=10 18.4% t<=100 39.2%
# beta   [29.1, 7.87, 1.08, 0.59] t<=10 12.8% t<=100 34.1%
# simple [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0] t<=10 0.9% t<=100 9.9%
# log-log slope, t = 2..100: -0.96
```

## Summary

1. Markov forward transitions and Gaussian closure give $q(x_t\mid x_0)=\mathcal N(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0,(1-\bar\alpha_t)I)$, the one-step renoising formula (@prp-forward-marginal).
2. The reverse process is approximated by Gaussian Markov transitions for small steps, and the upper bound on the negative log-likelihood decomposes, by Bayes' rule and a telescoping sum, into $L_T+\sum_{t\ge2}L_{t-1}+L_0$.
3. Completing the square gives the exact posterior $\mathcal N(\tilde\mu_t,\tilde\beta_tI)$ (@prp-posterior); rewriting $\tilde\mu_t$ with the one-step renoising formula turns mean prediction into the noise-estimation loss. Training is self-supervised.
4. In the fixed-variance DDPM considered here, ancestral sampling adds fresh noise $\sigma_tz$ to the mean, with $\sigma_t$ determined in closed form by the forward schedule; learned-variance variants relax this choice.
5. DDIM uses a non-Markovian family with the same marginals as DDPM, and keeps the same loss and the same noise estimator.
6. The DDPM reverse chain is always Markov. A Gaussian reverse step is, heuristically, accurate when the relative SNR drop per step, $\mathrm{SNR}(t-1)/\mathrm{SNR}(t)-1$, is small; for the linear schedule the drop is largest in the first steps (about 1.2 at $t=2$).
7. The simplified loss is a reweighting that sets the VLB coefficients $w_t$ to 1; in $x_0$-space the VLB weights each step by the SNR it loses, $\tfrac12(\mathrm{SNR}(t-1)-\mathrm{SNR}(t))$ (@eq-vlb-snr). The reweighting improves FID from 13.51 to 3.17 at the cost of NLL rising slightly from 3.70 to 3.75 bits/dim.
8. $\epsilon$-, $x_0$- and $v$-prediction are rotated coordinates of the same latent pair, and in $x_0$-space they weight the error by SNR, 1 and SNR+1.
9. DDIM becomes DDPM for $\gamma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$ and a deterministic sampler for $\gamma_t=0$. For every $\gamma>0$ its bound is a positively weighted noise-prediction MSE, so an ideal noise predictor serves every $\gamma$; DDIM can also skip steps along a subsequence, where deterministic sampling degrades least.

## Connections and further reading {#sec-further}

- **Latent-variable models.** The variational bound has the same structure as the VAE ELBO [@kingma2014, arXiv:1312.6114]. DDPM is a deep latent-variable model whose inference path is fixed rather than learned.
- **Continuous time.** Score-based SDEs place stochastic DDPM sampling and deterministic probability-flow sampling in a common continuous-time framework [@sde, arXiv:2011.13456].
- **Original papers.** Diffusion probabilistic models start with @sohl2015 [arXiv:1503.03585]; the DDPM derivation and the simplified loss are in @ho2020 [arXiv:2006.11239], Secs. 3--4; learned variances, the cosine schedule and the VLB analysis in @nichol2021 [arXiv:2102.09672]; the SNR form of the bound in @kingma2021 [arXiv:2107.00630]; DDIM in @ddim [arXiv:2010.02502], Secs. 3--5; $v$-prediction and loss weighting in @salimans2022 [arXiv:2202.00512], Sec. 4 and App. D; Noise2Score in @kim2021 [arXiv:2106.07009]; score matching and its denoising form in @hyvarinen2005 [JMLR 6, 695--709] and @vincent2011 [Neural Computation 23, 1661--1674].

## Appendix: proofs {#sec-proofs}

This appendix collects the longer proofs and algebraic checks of results stated in the main text.

### Gaussian lemmas {#sec-proof-lemmas}

**Proof of @lem-gauss-lin.** By independence the characteristic function factorizes, $\mathbb E\,e^{ik^{\mathsf T}(Au+Bv+c)}=e^{ik^{\mathsf T}c}\,\varphi_u(A^{\mathsf T}k)\,\varphi_v(B^{\mathsf T}k)$, and since $\varphi_u(k)=\exp(ik^{\mathsf T}m_u-\tfrac12k^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_uk)$ the product is $\exp\!\big(ik^{\mathsf T}(Am_u+Bm_v+c)-\tfrac12k^{\mathsf T}(A\Sigma_uA^{\mathsf T}+B\Sigma_vB^{\mathsf T})k\big)$, the characteristic function of the claimed Gaussian. $\square$

**Proof of @lem-complete-square.** Expanding the right-hand side gives $-\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Ax+x^{\mathsf T}h-\tfrac12h^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}h+\tfrac12h^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}h$, which is the left-hand side. The last term does not depend on $x$ and is absorbed into the normalizing constant. $\square$

**Proof of @lem-gauss-kl.** $\log q(x)-\log p(x)=\tfrac d2\log\tfrac{s_2^2}{s_1^2}-\tfrac{\lVert x-m_1\rVert^2}{2s_1^2}+\tfrac{\lVert x-m_2\rVert^2}{2s_2^2}$. Under $x\sim q$, $\mathbb E\lVert x-m_1\rVert^2=ds_1^2$, and since the cross term has zero mean, $\mathbb E\lVert x-m_2\rVert^2=\mathbb E\lVert(x-m_1)+(m_1-m_2)\rVert^2=ds_1^2+\lVert m_1-m_2\rVert^2$. Substituting gives @eq-gauss-kl. $\square$

### The reverse chain is Markov {#sec-proof-reverse-markov}

**Proof of @prp-reverse-markov.** If the forward chain is Markov, then $q(x_{t+1:T}\mid x_t,x_{t-1})=q(x_{t+1:T}\mid x_t)$, so

$$
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_{t:T})
=\frac{q(x_{t-1})\,q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\,q(x_{t+1:T}\mid x_t)}{q(x_t)\,q(x_{t+1:T}\mid x_t)}
=\frac{q(x_{t-1})\,q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})}{q(x_t)}
=q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t).
$$

The numerator is the chain rule for the joint, and the denominator is $q(x_{t:T})=q(x_t)\,q(x_{t+1:T}\mid x_t)$. No assumption on the step size is used. $\square$

### The Gaussian approximation for small steps (heuristic) {#sec-proof-small-step}

**Derivation of @eq-reverse-small-step.** This is a first-order approximation, not a rigorous proof. By Bayes' rule,

$$
\begin{aligned}
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
&=\frac{q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\,q_{t-1}(x_{t-1})}{q_t(x_t)}\\
&\propto_{x_{t-1}}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\alpha_t}{2\beta_t}\left\lVert x_{t-1}-m_t\right\rVert^2\right)q_{t-1}(x_{t-1}),
\qquad m_t:=\frac{x_t}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}},
\end{aligned}
$$

using $\lVert x_t-\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}\rVert^2=\alpha_t\lVert x_{t-1}-m_t\rVert^2$. The first factor is a Gaussian of width $\sqrt{\beta_t/\alpha_t}$, so for small $\beta_t$ the mass of $x_{t-1}$ is concentrated near $m_t$. Expanding there, $\log q_{t-1}(x_{t-1})=\log q_{t-1}(m_t)+g_t^{\mathsf T}(x_{t-1}-m_t)+r_t$ with $g_t:=\nabla\log q_{t-1}(m_t)$, where the remainder $r_t$ is of order $\tfrac12\lVert\nabla^2\log q_{t-1}\rVert\,\lVert x_{t-1}-m_t\rVert^2$. Dropping $r_t$ and applying @lem-complete-square with precision $A=(\alpha_t/\beta_t)I$ and linear term $h=(\alpha_t/\beta_t)m_t+g_t$ gives the mean $A^{-1}h=m_t+(\beta_t/\alpha_t)g_t$ and the covariance $(\beta_t/\alpha_t)I$.

Since $\lVert x_{t-1}-m_t\rVert^2\approx d\beta_t/\alpha_t$ in that region, the dropped $r_t$, compared with the Gaussian exponent $\tfrac{\alpha_t}{2\beta_t}\lVert x_{t-1}-m_t\rVert^2\approx d/2$, has relative size about $\beta_t\lVert\nabla^2\log q_{t-1}\rVert/\alpha_t$. If the data are sharply concentrated, $q_{t-1}$ is the data blurred by a Gaussian of variance $1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}$, so $\lVert\nabla^2\log q_{t-1}\rVert\approx1/(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})$. For data with several well-separated modes the curvature between the modes can be larger, so this is a scale rather than a bound. For Gaussian data $x_0\sim\mathcal N(0,s^2I)$ this can be checked exactly. Then $q_{t-1}=\mathcal N(0,\kappa I)$ with $\kappa:=\bar\alpha_{t-1}s^2+1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}$, the precision of the exact posterior is $\alpha_t/\beta_t+1/\kappa$, and with $\delta:=\beta_t/(\alpha_t\kappa)$ the exact mean and variance are $m_t/(1+\delta)$ and $(\beta_t/\alpha_t)/(1+\delta)$. @eq-reverse-small-step, with $\nabla\log q_{t-1}(m_t)=-m_t/\kappa$, gives the mean $m_t(1-\delta)$ and the variance $\beta_t/\alpha_t$. The means differ by $m_t\delta^2/(1+\delta)$, a relative error of $\delta^2$, while the approximate variance is too large by the relative amount $\delta$; both vanish as $\delta\to0$. As $s\to0$, $\delta=\beta_t/(\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}))$. Since $\mathrm{SNR}(t-1)/\mathrm{SNR}(t)=(1-\bar\alpha_t)/\big(\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})\big)$ and $(1-\bar\alpha_t)-\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})=1-\alpha_t=\beta_t$, this limit equals $\mathrm{SNR}(t-1)/\mathrm{SNR}(t)-1$, which is @eq-small-step-ratio.

### Decomposition of the variational bound {#sec-proof-vlb}

**Proof of @thm-vlb.** Start from the joint factorizations and justify each change of measure in turn.

*Step 1.* From @eq-forward-chain and @eq-reverse-joint, $\frac{p_\theta(x_{0:T})}{q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)}=p(x_T)\prod_{t=1}^{T}\frac{p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)}{q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})}$; taking logarithms gives @eq-vlb-sum.

*Step 2.* Separate the $t=1$ term $\log\frac{p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)}{q(x_1\mid x_0)}$ from the sum.

*Step 3.* For $t\ge2$ the Markov property gives $q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})=q(x_t\mid x_{t-1},x_0)$, and Bayes' rule for the two variables $(x_{t-1},x_t)$ conditioned on $x_0$ gives @eq-bayes-rearrange. Each term with $t\ge2$ becomes

$$
\log\frac{p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)}{q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})}
=\log\frac{p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)}{q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)}
+\log\frac{q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)}{q(x_t\mid x_0)}.
$$

At $t=1$, $x_{t-1}=x_0$ is itself the conditioning variable, so $q(x_0\mid x_1,x_0)$ degenerates to a point mass and this rewriting is not used. This is why the $t=1$ term was separated in step 2.

*Step 4.* Summing the second log-ratio over $t=2,\ldots,T$ telescopes to $\log q(x_1\mid x_0)-\log q(x_T\mid x_0)$. Combined with the $t=1$ term of step 2, $\log q(x_1\mid x_0)$ cancels, which gives the displayed equation in the main text.

*Step 5.* Substituting into @eq-vlb-sum and grouping $-\log p(x_T)+\log q(x_T\mid x_0)=-\log\frac{p(x_T)}{q(x_T\mid x_0)}$,

$$
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{VLB}}
=\mathbb E_q\!\left[
-\log\frac{p(x_T)}{q(x_T\mid x_0)}
-\sum_{t=2}^{T}\log\frac{p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)}{q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)}
-\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)
\right].
$$

*Step 6.* The integrand of each term with $t\ge2$ depends only on $(x_0,x_{t-1},x_t)$. Marginalizing $q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)$ onto $(x_{t-1},x_t)$ gives $q(x_{t-1},x_t\mid x_0)=q(x_t\mid x_0)\,q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)}\!\left[\log\frac{q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)}{p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)}\right]
&=\mathbb E_{q(x_t\mid x_0)}\!\left[
\int q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\log\frac{q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)}{p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)}\,dx_{t-1}
\right]\\
&=\mathbb E_{q(x_t\mid x_0)}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\,\Vert\,p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\right)\right].
\end{aligned}
$$

In the same way the first term becomes $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(x_T\mid x_0)\,\Vert\,p(x_T))$. Averaging over $x_0\sim q_{\mathrm{data}}$ gives @eq-vlb-decomposition. $\square$

### The constant term when the variances differ {#sec-proof-kl-constant}

**Proof of @eq-mean-matching.** Substituting $m_1=\tilde\mu_t$, $s_1^2=\tilde\beta_t$, $m_2=\mu_\theta$, $s_2^2=\sigma_t^2$ into @lem-gauss-kl,

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\,\Vert\,p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\right)
=\frac{\lVert\tilde\mu_t-\mu_\theta\rVert^2}{2\sigma_t^2}
+\underbrace{\frac d2\left[\frac{\tilde\beta_t}{\sigma_t^2}-1+\log\frac{\sigma_t^2}{\tilde\beta_t}\right]}_{C_t}.
$$

With $\xi:=\tilde\beta_t/\sigma_t^2$ the bracket is $\xi-1-\log\xi\ge0$, with equality only at $\xi=1$, so $C_t\ge0$, with equality only when $\sigma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$. Taking the expectation over $q$ gives @eq-mean-matching. $\square$

### An optimum that does not depend on the weights {#sec-proof-bayes}

**Proof of @eq-bayes-optimal.** For fixed $t$ and any function $f$, the tower property makes the cross term $\mathbb E[(\epsilon-\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t])^{\mathsf T}(\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t]-f(x_t))]$ vanish, so

$$
\mathbb E\lVert\epsilon-f(x_t)\rVert^2
=\mathbb E\lVert\epsilon-\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t]\rVert^2
+\mathbb E\lVert\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t]-f(x_t)\rVert^2.
$$

The second term vanishes only for $f=\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t]$. If $\epsilon_\theta(\cdot,t)$ can represent an arbitrary function independently for each $t$, the minimizer of the sum weighted by $\lambda_t>0$ is the same $\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t]$ at every time. $\square$

### The score identity and Tweedie's formula {#sec-proof-tweedie}

**Proof of @eq-epsilon-score-conversion.** Exchanging differentiation and integration (justified by dominated convergence, since for the Gaussian kernel $\nabla_{x_t}q(x_t\mid x_0)$ is bounded uniformly in $x_0$; no moment condition on the data is needed),

$$
\nabla\log q_t(x_t)
=\frac{\int q_{\mathrm{data}}(x_0)\,q(x_t\mid x_0)\,\nabla_{x_t}\log q(x_t\mid x_0)\,dx_0}{q_t(x_t)}
=\mathbb E\!\left[\nabla_{x_t}\log q(x_t\mid x_0)\,\middle|\,x_t\right].
$$

From @eq-forward-marginal, $\nabla_{x_t}\log q(x_t\mid x_0)=-(x_t-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0)/(1-\bar\alpha_t)=-\epsilon/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$, which gives the first identity, and the optimal predictor is $\epsilon^*=\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t]$ of @eq-bayes-optimal. The second identity follows by taking the conditional expectation given $x_t$ of $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon$, which gives $\mathbb E[x_0\mid x_t]=(x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t])/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$, and substituting the first identity. @eq-ddpm-mean-score follows directly by substituting $\epsilon_\theta=-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,s_\theta$ into @eq-epsilon-parameterization, since $-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\epsilon_\theta=\beta_ts_\theta$. The one-step identity @eq-one-step-tweedie follows from the same argument: exchanging differentiation and integration in $q_t(x_t)=\int q_{t-1}(x_{t-1})\,\mathcal N(x_t;\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1},\beta_tI)\,dx_{t-1}$ gives

$$
\nabla\log q_t(x_t)
=\mathbb E\!\left[-\frac{x_t-\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}}{\beta_t}\,\middle|\,x_t\right]
=-\frac{x_t-\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,\mathbb E[x_{t-1}\mid x_t]}{\beta_t},
$$

which is solved for $\mathbb E[x_{t-1}\mid x_t]$. $\square$

### The DDIM objective is a weighted noise-prediction loss {#sec-proof-ddim-objective}

**Proof of @eq-ddim-weights.** This proves Theorem 1 of @ddim [App. B] in this note's notation. Their generative model has $p(x_T)=\mathcal N(0,I)$, the transitions $p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t):=q_\gamma(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,\hat x_0(x_t,t))$ for $t\ge2$, which is the step @eq-ddim-step, and a Gaussian decoder $p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)=\mathcal N(\hat x_0(x_1,1),\gamma_1^2I)$ with $\gamma_1>0$ (Sec. 3.2, Eq. 10). Since $q_\gamma(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=q_\gamma(x_T\mid x_0)\prod_{t=2}^{T}q_\gamma(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$ is already written in reverse order,

$$
\log\frac{q_\gamma(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)}{p_\theta(x_{0:T})}
=\log\frac{q_\gamma(x_T\mid x_0)}{p(x_T)}
+\sum_{t=2}^{T}\log\frac{q_\gamma(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)}{p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)}
-\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1),
$$

and taking expectations as in step 6 of @sec-proof-vlb turns the first two groups into KL divergences. The first does not depend on $\theta$.

For $t\ge2$ write the mean of @eq-ddim-posterior as $c_tx_0+e_tx_t$ with $e_t:=\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\gamma_t^2}/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$. The generative mean is $c_t\hat x_0+e_tx_t$, so the two means differ by $c_t(x_0-\hat x_0)$. From $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$ and @eq-epsilon-to-x0, $x_0-\hat x_0=\big(\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)-\epsilon\big)/\sqrt{\mathrm{SNR}(t)}$. Both covariances are $\gamma_t^2I$, so @lem-gauss-kl gives the KL divergence $c_t^2\lVert x_0-\hat x_0\rVert^2/(2\gamma_t^2)=\lambda_t\lVert\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta\rVert^2$ with $\lambda_t$ of @eq-ddim-weights. By @prp-ddim-marginal, $x_t\sim q_\gamma(x_t\mid x_0)$ is the one-step renoising of $x_0$ for every $\gamma$, so the expectation runs over the same $(x_0,\epsilon)$ as in $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}$. In the same way $-\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)=\lVert\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_1,1)\rVert^2/(2\gamma_1^2\,\mathrm{SNR}(1))+\text{const}$. Altogether the bound equals $\sum_{t=1}^{T}\lambda_t\,\mathbb E\lVert\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\rVert^2+C$ with $\lambda_1:=1/(2\gamma_1^2\,\mathrm{SNR}(1))$ and a constant $C$.

*Positivity.* $c_t$ increases with $\gamma_t$. At $\gamma_t=0$, multiplying by $\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$ shows that $c_t>0$ is equivalent to $\bar\alpha_{t-1}(1-\bar\alpha_t)>(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})\bar\alpha_t$, that is, to $\bar\alpha_{t-1}>\bar\alpha_t$, which holds because $\alpha_t<1$. Hence $\lambda_t>0$ for every $\gamma_t>0$.

*Check.* For $\gamma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$, @sec-proof-ddim-ddpm gives $c_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\beta_t/(1-\bar\alpha_t)$. With $\tilde\beta_t=(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})\beta_t/(1-\bar\alpha_t)$ and $\bar\alpha_{t-1}/\bar\alpha_t=1/\alpha_t$,

$$
\lambda_t
=\frac{\bar\alpha_{t-1}\beta_t^2}{(1-\bar\alpha_t)^2}
\cdot\frac{1-\bar\alpha_t}{2(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})\beta_t}
\cdot\frac{1-\bar\alpha_t}{\bar\alpha_t}
=\frac{\beta_t}{2\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}
=w_t. \qquad\square
$$

### Reduction of DDIM to DDPM {#sec-proof-ddim-ddpm}

**Proof of @prp-ddim-ddpm.** The variances agree by definition, so it suffices to compare the coefficients of the mean. Using $\tilde\beta_t=(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})\beta_t/(1-\bar\alpha_t)$ and $1-\bar\alpha_t-\beta_t=\alpha_t-\bar\alpha_t=\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\tilde\beta_t
&=(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})\frac{1-\bar\alpha_t-\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}
=\frac{\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})^2}{1-\bar\alpha_t},\\
\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\tilde\beta_t}&=\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

So the coefficient of $x_t$ in the mean of @eq-ddim-posterior is $\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})/(1-\bar\alpha_t)$, as in @eq-posterior-mean, and, using $\sqrt{\alpha_t}\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}=\alpha_t\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}$, the coefficient of $x_0$ is

$$
\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}-\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}
=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\frac{(1-\bar\alpha_t)-\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}
=\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t},
$$

which also agrees. Both generative steps substitute the same $\hat x_0$ for $x_0$, and $(x_t-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\hat x_0)/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}=\epsilon_\theta$, so @eq-ddpm-in-ddim-form has the same mean as @eq-ddpm-sampling. $\square$
